sens: To be a disciple of someone, to follow them and learn from them
To make someone a disciple, to instruct them in faith and Christian living
To be taught, trained in a doctrine or practice
G3100.detail:
1. In the passive or intransitive sense, it means to be attached to someone as a disciple: to learn from them, to follow them, to live according to their teaching. Joseph of Arimathea was a disciple of Jesus (Matthew 27:57), which means he chose to follow and believe in Him.

2. In the active and transitive sense, it means to transform someone into a disciple: to teach them, to train them in the Christian faith. Jesus commands His apostles: "Make disciples of all nations" (Matthew 28:19), which means to instruct the peoples, to lead them to believe and obey.

3. It also means to be trained, instructed in a doctrine: a scribe "instructed" in the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 13:52) is one who has learned and understood the realities of God's kingdom, and can therefore draw out old and new treasures for others.
G3100.origine: The word comes from "mathêtês" (disciple), which is itself formed from the root meaning "to learn" or "to understand." It is a verb created to express the process of learning and formation: not just receiving information, but becoming a follower, a companion who changes their life. The verb belongs to an action family where the "disciple" is not a mere listener, but someone who is transformed, shaped.
G3100.emploi: The verb is infrequent in the New Testament (4 occurrences). In Matthew, it first appears to describe Joseph of Arimathea who was already a disciple of Jesus (27:57), then in the Great Commission where Jesus sends the apostles to "make disciples of all nations" (28:19), showing that the mission consists of forming new disciples. In Luke, in Acts 14:21, Paul and Barnabas make disciples by preaching the Gospel in the cities. A final usage in Matthew speaks of being "instructed" in the kingdom of heaven (13:52), highlighting that the disciple is someone educated, trained.
G3100.portee: This word is at the heart of the Christian missionary mandate. Jesus does not merely ask to preach, but to "make disciples": that is, to accompany believers so they learn to know Him, to obey Him, and to live in the kingdom of God. It reminds Christians that their faith is not an isolated adherence, but a continuous learning, a lasting transformation.

sens: one who learns from a master, who follows him to receive his teaching
one who adheres to a master and shares his cause
each of the twelve apostles chosen by Jesus
every Christian who follows Jesus
G3101.detail:
1. A disciple is primarily a learner: he sits at the feet of a master to listen and retain his teaching. Matthew 5:1 shows the disciples approaching Jesus sitting on the mountain to listen to Him. The word emphasizes this learning relationship: the disciple is not an equal, but someone who receives, who grows in knowledge and the ability to do what the master does.
2. To be a disciple is also a personal adherence to the master and his cause: the disciple abandons what he was doing to follow (Matthew 8:21-23 shows men who want to first bury their father before following Jesus). It is a break with the former life, a loyalty that requires sacrifice.
3. Jesus chose twelve particular disciples (Matthew 10:1) — the apostles — who remain by His side, receive His private teaching (Matthew 13:36), and participate in His work (Matthew 14:19, where they distribute food to the crowd).
4. From Acts onward, "disciple" designates any believer who follows Jesus after the resurrection (Acts 6:1, 9:19), which shows the expansion: every Christian becomes a disciple of the Lord, learning to live according to His teaching.
G3101.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "to learn" (μανθάνω) and literally means "one who learns." Its equivalent in the Greek Old Testament translates Hebrew words related to apprentices or servants of a prophet. It is a living word from the ancient world: every philosopher, every master had his disciples, his students who constituted his school.
G3101.emploi: This word appears 251 times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. In the Gospels, it first designates the direct companions of Jesus: the twelve (Matthew 10:1, 11:1), but also a larger group (Matthew 5:1, John 6:66). The disciples have varied roles: they listen to Jesus' teaching (Matthew 13:36), question Him to understand (Matthew 15:12), serve Him (Mark 6:45), distribute food (John 6:11). After the resurrection and starting from Acts, every believer in Jesus is called a disciple, which universalizes the term: it no longer describes just a personal relationship with the Christ living on earth, but the commitment of every Christian to Him.
G3101.portee: The word "disciple" reminds today's Christian that their faith is not passive: it is a continuous learning from a master, Jesus. To be a disciple requires listening, retaining, and putting into practice. It also implies a certain break with the priorities of the world — there is a cost to following. But it also means that one is never alone in this learning: Jesus' disciples learn together, support each other, and participate in His mission.

sens: a woman who follows the teaching of a master
a woman who believes in Jesus and follows Him
a woman engaged in the service of God
G3102.detail:
1. A female disciple is a woman who follows the teaching of a master and learns from him. The Greek word literally means "she who learns": it is the feminine equivalent of disciple in the masculine form. In Acts 9:36, Tabitha (or Dorcas) is called a disciple because she believed in Jesus and walked in His footsteps.
2. More broadly, a female disciple is a woman who believes in Jesus Christ and commits to following Him. She recognizes His authority and teaching, and seeks to live according to His words.
3. In the context of the early Church, it is a woman who manifests her faith through concrete actions: Tabitha was known for her good works and alms, showing that her faith translated into action and service to others.
G3102.origine: The word comes from the Greek mathêtria, formed from mathêtês (disciple), which itself derives from the verb manthanô (to learn). It is the regular feminine form of the masculine term μαθητής. The word expresses the idea of a person engaged in a learning process with a master, with a lasting relationship and personal commitment.
G3102.emploi: The word mathêtria appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 9:36, to designate Tabitha. This unique occurrence shows that women as well as men could be disciples of Jesus and be part of the early Christian community. Although the term is rare, it reveals that the nascent Church recognized and valued believing women as full disciples, capable of authentic spiritual commitment and a ministry of service.
G3102.portee: This unique mention of Tabitha as a disciple affirms an important truth for the Christian faith: women are disciples of Christ on the same level as men. Her example reminds us that discipleship is measured not by gender, but by faith in Jesus and by the works of love and service that flow from it. It is an invitation for every believer, man or woman, to fully live their commitment to Christ in action and generosity.

sens: Biblical character, antediluvian man from the Old Testament
Ancestor of Noah in the genealogy of Adam
G3103.detail: Methuselah is a patriarch from the antediluvian era, mentioned in the genealogy that traces back from Christ to Adam (Luke 3:37). He is the son of Enoch and the father of Lamech, and he became famous in tradition as the man who lived the longest: according to Genesis 5:27, he lived to be 969 years old. As an ancestor of Noah, he also appears in the genealogy of Genesis 5, making him an important link in the chain of transmission of the divine promise of salvation through the generations before the flood.
G3103.origine: The Hebrew name מְתוּשֶׁלַח (Methoushélah) likely means "man of the javelin" or "sent by God," according to interpretations from Hebrew tradition. It is a compound name from ancient Hebrew, characteristic of the antediluvian patriarchs. The name was transliterated into Greek as Μαθουσάλα (Mathousala) in the Septuagint and is referenced in the New Testament.
G3103.emploi: Methuselah appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:37, in the official genealogy of Jesus that traces back to Adam. Luke lists the ancestors of Christ generation by generation, and Methuselah is included as the son of Enoch and the father of Lamech. This mention integrates the characters of the antediluvian Old Testament into the story of salvation and establishes continuity between Adam and Noah, from whom all current humanity descends.
G3103.portee: The presence of Methuselah in the genealogy of Jesus reminds us that Christ is the fulfillment of a promise that spans all of human history, from creation to the days of the incarnation. It also emphasizes that even those who lived before the complete revelation in Christ are part of God's plan of salvation.

sens: son of Melea and father of Mattatha in the genealogy of Jesus
G3104.detail: Menna is an ancestor of Jesus according to the genealogy reported by Luke. He appears only once in the Gospel, in the genealogical list that traces Jesus' descent from David. His name is listed between those of Melea (his father) and Mattatha (his son), in this chain of ancestors that establishes that Jesus, although being the Son of God, is part of human history and the lineage of David.
G3104.origine: The name Menna (or Menna in some Greek manuscripts) is of Hebrew origin, although its exact meaning is not definitively established. It is a name borne in ancient Judea.
G3104.emploi: Menna appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:31, in the genealogy of Jesus. Unlike Matthew, who also provides the genealogy of the Messiah from David, Luke traces a different version, and Menna is included as a link in this chain of legitimate ancestors.

sens: To lose reason, to rave or speak nonsensically.
To be beside oneself, to behave in an extravagant or incomprehensible manner.
To appear unreasonable or insane in the eyes of others.
G3105.detail:
1. To be mad means to have lost the normal use of one's reason and to act irrationally. When people say that Jesus is mad (John 10:20), they imply that he speaks or acts without logic, that his words make no sense. It is the idea of a mind that wanders, losing touch with reality.

2. To be mad can also describe someone who speaks or acts in such a strange way that they seem to have lost control of themselves. Rhoda, the servant, seems mad to those who hear her claim that Peter is at the door (Acts 12:15): she asserts something so implausible, so contrary to expectations, that others take her for deranged.

3. Finally, to be mad is to appear unreasonable or insane to an audience. Festus accuses Paul of being mad (Acts 26:24) because his discourse on resurrection and Jesus Christ shocks ordinary human reason. Similarly, if all Christians speak in tongues in a gathering, non-believers will think they are mad (1 Corinthians 14:23): the behavior seems incomprehensible and unreasonable to those who do not understand the faith.
G3105.origine: The verb μαίνομαι comes from a root that evokes the idea of wandering and loss of control. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it sometimes translates הָלַל (to rave) and שָׁגַע (to be mad, to rave): the image is of a disturbed mind that wanders. The Greek verb literally designates the behavior of one who no longer masters their reason, who speaks or acts without logical coherence.
G3105.emploi: The verb appears about 5 times in the New Testament, always to describe a judgment made about someone: they are called mad. Jesus is called mad by those who do not understand his teaching (John 10:20). Rhoda is judged mad because she reports something that no one believes (Acts 12:15). Paul defends himself against Festus' accusation of being mad, asserting instead that his words are of truth and sound reasoning (Acts 26:24-25). In 1 Corinthians 14:23, the word describes how non-believers would perceive charismatics if they all spoke in tongues at once: as insane. Each time, the verb marks a disconnect between what someone says or does and what others find reasonable.
G3105.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on what the world considers madness and what God considers wisdom. Jesus, accused of madness by those who reject his message, and Paul, defending the resurrection against the disbelief of his time, remind us that faith in Christ may seem unreasonable to the carnal mind. It is an invitation not to fear being called mad for choosing to follow Christ, for this supposed madness is in reality the greatest wisdom.

sens: To call someone happy, blessed
To recognize and celebrate someone's blessed condition
To esteem and declare that someone is favored by God
G3106.detail:
1. The verb literally means "to call blessed" or "to proclaim happy." It is to acknowledge aloud, affirming that someone enjoys a condition of deep happiness (Luke 1:48: Mary says that generations will call her blessed).
2. This goes beyond a simple judgment: it is to actively celebrate someone's happy condition, particularly when it comes from God. For example, in James 5:11, we proclaim blessed those who have suffered patiently, because they have experienced the Lord's mercy.
3. The word also implies a recognition of divine favoritism: the one who is proclaimed blessed is presented as being filled by God, as having received his blessings.
G3106.origine: The verb comes from the adjective μακάριος (makarios, "blessed, happy"), which describes a deep happiness, often linked to divine blessings. The form with the suffix -ίζω (-izo) makes it an active verb: not just to be blessed (passive state), but to proclaim someone blessed (action). In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this verb commonly translates the verb אָשַׁר (ashar, "to call happy"), particularly in the beatitudes and hymns of praise.
G3106.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, always in the sense of "to proclaim blessed." In Luke 1:48, Mary anticipates that future generations will proclaim her blessed because of the great work God is accomplishing in her (the incarnation). In James 5:11, the apostle encourages believers to proclaim blessed those who endured suffering with patience, for the Lord ultimately shows them his mercy and compassion (as with Job). In both instances, proclaiming someone blessed is to recognize God's works in their life.
G3106.portee: This verb invites us to see how God acts in the lives of those who trust him, even in humiliation or suffering. It reminds us that true blessedness comes from God's work and deserves to be proclaimed and celebrated. It is also a call to discern and honor those in whom God manifests his grace and faithfulness.

sens: one who enjoys a good, a favor, an enviable condition
one who experiences deep joy, contentment
one who benefits from God's favor, blessing
one who receives a moral or spiritual blessing despite trials
G3107.detail:
1. The word primarily designates someone who possesses a good, a circumstance, or a condition that many envy: it is the man to whom sin is not imputed (Romans 4:8), or the one who receives what he cannot repay — a true favor.
2. It applies to one who feels satisfaction, a contentment that comes from his condition: the one who receives help, the one who is invited to the Lord's feast experiences profound joy.
3. It is one whom God blesses or favors in a special way — God Almighty himself is called "blessed" (1 Timothy 1:11) because he possesses fullness.
4. Finally, and this is the most astonishing aspect in the Gospel, the word applies to those who suffer for righteousness or for Christ: they are blessed, not because their external condition is enviable, but because they know God's hidden favor and participate in his kingdom (Matthew 5:3-11, 1 Peter 3:14).
G3107.origine: The word makarios comes from an ancient root that evokes the state of the gods and the blessed in Greek mythology — a condition of happiness. The Bible uses it to translate the Hebrew word asher, which literally means "who is well" or "who possesses good." It is not a happiness dependent on current circumstances, but a state of grace, a happy condition conferred by God.
G3107.emploi: The word appears 49 times in the New Testament, very often in the mouth of Jesus to proclaim a blessing. The Beatitudes (Matthew 5:3-12 and Luke 6:20-22) are at the heart of it: they enumerate who is blessed in God's eyes. Paul uses it to describe the state of one whose sins are not imputed (Romans 4:7-8) or one who does not condemn himself (Romans 14:22). Revelation uses it seven times at the conclusion of visions to confirm: "Blessed is he who..." (1:3, 14:13, 16:15, 19:9, 20:6, 22:7, 22:14). James links happiness to the one who perseveres under trial (James 1:12) or who keeps the Law (James 1:25). The word also applies to God and to the one who believes without seeing (John 20:29).
G3107.portee: For the believer, this word reveals that true happiness does not come from the absence of suffering, but from the relationship with God and obedience to his word. The Beatitudes challenge our view of happiness: they place it alongside the poor, the mourners, the persecuted, not because poverty or persecution are good in themselves, but because God is with those who seek him in these conditions. It is an invitation to seek contentment not in visible goods, but in God's hidden and unshakeable favor.

sens: The state of one who is declared blessed and favored by God
The expression, the proclamation of this state of divine favor
The congratulation, the wish for happiness addressed to someone
G3108.detail:
1. The happiness referred to by this word is primarily a blessing granted by God himself: it is the state of one to whom God recognizes righteousness, not by his works, but by faith. David describes it in Romans 4:6, where the apostle Paul shows that true happiness comes from God who imputes righteousness apart from works.

2. This happiness is not just an inner feeling, but something that is expressed, that is proclaimed aloud. In Galatians 4:15, Paul asks the Galatians: "Where then is your expression of happiness?" — he speaks of the living and visible testimony of their state of favor with God.

3. The word can also designate the congratulation addressed to one who is blessed, a word of acclaim or a wish for happiness. This is what Paul implicitly asks: that the Galatians, once so happy and expressive in their faith, maintain that radiant joy.
G3108.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to call happy" or "to declare blessed." It is formed from the root of the adjective "blessed, fortunate," which evokes one to whom all goes well, who enjoys divine favor. It is not a fleeting happiness or one due to chance, but the stable blessing that only God can give. The idea is found in the beatitudes ("blessed..."), where Jesus calls blessed those he recognizes.
G3108.emploi: This word appears only three times in the New Testament, all in Paul's epistles. In Romans 4:6 and 4:9, Paul uses it to describe the happiness of the believer justified by faith, and he emphasizes that this happiness belongs equally to the uncircumcised and the circumcised — the only criterion is faith. In Galatians 4:15, Paul refers to the happiness that the Galatians once expressed enthusiastically when they received it. In all cases, the word designates a state of blessing, a condition of favor with God, related to justification and the relationship with the Lord.
G3108.portee: This word reminds the Christian that true wealth is not material possession or social success, but the blessing of God who declares us righteous and accepted. It is an invitation not to hide this joy, but to express it, to testify. The Galatians understood this for a moment; Paul exhorts them to regain that joyful expression of their trust in God. For us today, it is a call to live in the certainty of the happiness of being loved and justified by the Lord.

sens: region in northern Greece
land from which the first European believers of Paul came
place of passage and ministry for the apostle Paul
G3109.detail:
1. Macedonia is a region of northern Greece, in ancient Balkans. It is there that Paul sees in a vision a Macedonian man crying out to him: "Come over to Macedonia and help us!" (Acts 16:9). This vision calls him to cross the Aegean Sea and preach the Gospel in Europe for the first time.

2. Macedonia is the cradle of the primitive Church in Europe. Its churches, notably that of Philippi, become a model of faith and generosity: the Macedonians give generously beyond their means (2 Corinthians 8:1-3). The apostle Paul speaks of it as a living example of God's grace.

3. It is a territory that Paul traverses and visits several times, sometimes to preach, sometimes to strengthen the churches. Silas and Timothy come from Macedonia to join Paul (Acts 18:5), and the region becomes a strategic place for his missionary work in Greece.
G3109.origine: The name "Macedonia" comes from ancient Greek and historically designates the kingdom of Macedonia, whose most famous rulers are Philip II and his son Alexander the Great. In the New Testament, it is the region where Paul establishes the first Christian churches in Europe, thus forever transforming this name into a symbol of the expansion of the Gospel beyond Israel.
G3109.emploi: The word "Macedonia" appears 21 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in the writings of Paul and the Acts that recount his ministry. Macedonia is primarily the place of the visionary call that sends Paul to Europe (Acts 16:9-10). It then becomes the theater of his first European missionary journey, where the churches of Philippi, Thessalonica, and Berea are born. Paul traverses it several times (Acts 20:1-3, 1 Corinthians 16:5) to teach and support the young churches. Macedonia and Achaia are often mentioned together as the two provinces of Greece where Paul planted the Gospel (Acts 19:21, Romans 15:26). Finally, the churches of Macedonia are renowned for their generosity and living faith, serving as a model for other communities.
G3109.portee: Macedonia reminds the Christian that God calls his people to cross borders to proclaim the Gospel. What Paul accomplished by obeying the vision of the Macedonian opened the way for the Christian faith in Europe and, subsequently, to the whole world. It is also a region whose churches embody the virtues of grace — generosity, perseverance, and joy in trust — that the believer is invited to cultivate.

sens: Inhabitant or native of Macedonia
Person of Macedonian nationality or origin
G3110.detail: 1. It refers to an inhabitant or native of Macedonia, the region in northeastern ancient Greece. Paul encounters a Macedonian in a vision who calls him to come preach in his region (Acts 16:9). 2. The term also designates Paul's companions from Macedonia, such as Aristarchus of Thessalonica, who traveled with him (Acts 19:29 and 27:2). 3. By extension, it relates to the Macedonian churches and Christians: Paul praises the generosity of the Macedonians to the Christians in Achaia to encourage them to give generously to the poor (2 Corinthians 9:2-4).
G3110.origine: The Greek word Μακεδών comes from Μακεδονία (Macedonia), the name of the ancient region located in northern Greece. This suffix "-ών" is the usual ending to designate the inhabitants of a country or city: it functions like our French suffix "-ien" (Parisian, Marseillais). Macedonia was a powerful Greek kingdom, with Philip and Alexander the Great being its most famous rulers.
G3110.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the New Testament, only in Acts and in Paul's letters to the Corinthians. It first refers to the man in the vision who calls Paul to come preach (Acts 16:9). Then, it names the actual companions of Paul from Macedonia (Acts 19:29; 27:2), notably Aristarchus. Finally, Paul uses it to speak of the Macedonian churches, whose generosity serves as an example to encourage the Corinthians to charity (2 Corinthians 9:2, 4). It is a concrete word, without particular theological connotation: it simply identifies the place of origin or nationality.
G3110.portee: This word shows us how the Gospel spread in the region of Macedonia and beyond. The call of the Macedonian in the vision is a decisive turning point: it prompts Paul to cross the Aegean Sea and bring the Good News to Europe (Acts 16:9-10). The Macedonians also represent an example of generous faith and sharing: their churches, although poor, gave generously for the assistance of the poor in Jerusalem (2 Corinthians 9:2-4). Their zeal should inspire every Christian to give selflessly and support brothers in need.

sens: Place where meat and other food items are sold
Public space for commercial exchanges in a city
G3111.detail: 1. A meat market is a place where merchants sell meat and other provisions at retail for daily consumption. In 1 Corinthians 10:25, Paul encourages Christians to buy freely what is sold there, without excessive guilt: the market is simply a normal supply place. 2. More broadly, it is a public urban market, a center of exchanges and commerce where sellers and buyers are active; it was a common institution in Greco-Roman cities.
G3111.origine: The Greek word μάκελλον comes from the Latin macellum, borrowed by the Greeks who lived in contact with Rome and in the Roman Empire. It properly designates a market or butcher shop, that is, a building or space arranged for the sale of provisions. This vocabulary reflects the urban and commercial life of the Mediterranean world in the first century.
G3111.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 10:25. Paul uses it in his practical response to a question of Christian ethics: faced with meat from pagan sacrifices, believers can buy at the market without torturing their conscience. The context is that of Christian freedoms and respect for weak consciences. This passage shows that Paul considers the market as a place of ordinary and acceptable life, where the believer can shop without scruple.
G3111.portee: This verse reminds every Christian that they live in the ordinary world and can accept its practical institutions without fear, provided their conscience is right before God. Paul frees us from a paralyzing guilt over the details of daily life, as long as we do not violate charity towards our weak brothers. It is a word of wisdom and freedom for those who doubt.

sens: At a great distance in space
At a considerable distance (duration, measure)
Separated, distant (figuratively)
Strange, excluded (spiritually or socially)
G3112.detail:
1. The word designates a great spatial distance: the father of the prodigal son sees him coming "from afar" (Luke 15:20), and the disciples' boat is "far" from land (John 21:8). It is the measurable distance that one can travel.
2. It also applies to what lasts or extends for a long time: the "long" prayers of the Pharisees (Matthew 23:14) are prayers that take a lot of time.
3. Spiritually, it expresses the distance from the kingdom of God: Jesus tells the scribe that he is "not far" from the kingdom (Mark 12:34), using this distance as an image of the inner state, the lack or proximity to God.
4. It describes those who are "far" from God or excluded from His covenant: the Gentiles far from the promise of Israel (Acts 2:39), or the Gentiles who were once strangers but are now brought near in Christ (Ephesians 2:13, 2:17).
G3112.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective μακρός (long, distant). The expression "far" was originally constructed with the word for "way" (ὁδόν) implied: "a long way," hence "far." In Hebrew and Aramaic, the word conveyed the idea of distance (רָחוֹק, "distant"). The Greek verb μακρύνειν (to lengthen, to extend) and the noun μακρότης (length) belong to the same family.
G3112.emploi: This word appears about eleven times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and Paul's epistles. Literally, it measures a distance: a herd is "far" (Matthew 8:30), a boat has drifted from the shore (John 21:8), Jesus is "hardly far" from a house (Luke 7:6). Figuratively, it becomes crucial in Pauline theology: in Ephesians, Paul uses it to describe the Gentiles who were once "far" from the covenant, whom Christ has brought near (Ephesians 2:13, 2:17). Mark 12:34 uses it to express spiritual distance from the kingdom, not as a condemnation, but as an encouraging proximity. The word often translates the Hebrew רָחוֹק in the Greek of the Old Testament.
G3112.portee: This word reveals how the Bible measures distances: not only physical space but also the distance from God. For the believer, it reminds us that conversion erases this spiritual distance. In Ephesians, it highlights the work of Christ who has brought the far ones near: it is a source of hope for all those who felt excluded from the divine promise. The word invites us to measure our closeness to the heart of God, not by perfection, but by our attachment to Christ.

sens: At a great distance in space
Observing or following someone without getting closer
Maintaining a certain distance out of respect, fear, or embarrassment
G3113.detail:
1. The simplest meaning: at a great physical distance. When Mark says that Jesus saw a fig tree from afar, it means he noticed it while still far away (Mark 11:13).

2. The word also describes the act of looking at, following, or observing someone from a distance, without touching or really getting close. Peter followed Jesus from afar to the courtyard of the high priest (Matthew 26:58); the women at the foot of the cross looked on from afar (Mark 15:40).

3. It can express a moral or emotional distance: the distance imposed by fear, respect, or shame. The tax collector stood at a distance, not daring to lift his eyes (Luke 18:13). In Revelation, the merchants stand far off from Babylon, seized with terror (Revelation 18:10).
G3113.origine: The word comes from the Greek μακρός (makros, "long, large") combined with the suffix -θεν which indicates the point of departure or place ("from where," "from"). It literally means "from the distant (point)." The Greek word reflects the Hebrew רָחוֹק (rahok, "far") and the verb רָחַק (rahaq, "to distance oneself"), found in the Psalms and the Old Testament.
G3113.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke). It primarily describes a physical distance: seeing something or someone from afar. But it also takes on an emotional hue: Peter follows Jesus from afar out of fear of compromising himself, and the women at the cross remain at a distance out of pain and caution. In Revelation 18, "from afar" emphasizes the terror of the merchants fleeing Babylon. The word is neutral — it is the situation that imbues the distance with a moral or emotional significance.
G3113.portee: This word reminds us that faith does not require physical proximity to Jesus, but rather the heart. The tax collector who stands afar, not lifting his eyes, receives justification (Luke 18:13): God sees humility and repentance, not the position of the body. It also speaks to us of the fear of the Lord — a respectful fear that keeps us at a distance of reverence while allowing us to look toward Him.

sens: To bear someone with calmness and kindness, without becoming irritated or rushed
To wait without impatience, to persevere despite delays
To endure a difficult situation with constancy
G3114.detail:
1. To have patience toward someone means to bear them gently, without anger and without haste. It is the virtue opposed to quickness to anger or to take revenge. In the parable of the unforgiving servant, the king shows patience by allowing the servant to request a delay to repay his debt (Matthew 18:26 and 18:29). Charity, as Paul describes, is patient — it endures the faults of others (1 Corinthians 13:4).
2. To have patience also means to wait, without becoming discouraged, for the fulfillment of a promise or justice. Abraham persevered, meaning he waited with confidence, and obtained the realization of God's promise (Hebrews 6:15). God Himself shows patience toward us, delaying His judgment because He desires that all come to repentance (2 Peter 3:9).
3. To have patience also means to endure a trying situation with constancy and without complaint. James encourages believers to be patient, to remain steadfast, while waiting for the coming of the Lord (James 5:7-8). This patience is a moral strength that combats discouragement and abandonment.
G3114.origine: The Greek word comes from two compound words: makros (long, enduring) and thumos (the heart, soul, temperament, particularly anger). Literally, "to have a long heart" or "to have a heart that takes time to ignite." This image comes from the Hebrew arek aph (literally "slow to anger"), which describes patience as long-suffering — a capacity to restrain anger and endure for a long time. This is why the word naturally opposes impatience, quick anger, and irritability.
G3114.emploi: The verb makrothumeō appears 9 times in the New Testament, mainly in the epistles and the Gospels. It is primarily used in two ways: (1) to have patience toward someone (Matthew 18:26, 29; 1 Thessalonians 5:14), and (2) to wait patiently or persevere in trials (1 Corinthians 13:4; Hebrews 6:15; James 5:7-8; 2 Peter 3:9). Paul places it at the heart of Christian love (1 Corinthians 13:4). James encourages it in the face of present sufferings by reminding of the Lord's return. The word denotes a highly valued moral virtue in biblical ethics.
G3114.portee: Patience is not passivity or weakness, but a virtue of the heart that reflects the character of God Himself. It requires inner strength to master one's anger, to bear with others, and to remain confident when everything seems delayed. It is a grace given to those who believe in God and hope for His intervention, knowing that the Lord is coming back.

sens: Ability to endure trials and difficulties for a long time without becoming discouraged
Quality of one who remains calm in the face of constraints, delays, or offenses
Virtue of perseverance and steadfastness in faith and effort
God's restraint in not punishing the sinner immediately, allowing time for repentance
G3115.detail: 1. Patience is primarily the strength to endure trials without giving up: it is holding firm when everything becomes difficult. In Hebrews 6:12, Christians are called to imitate those who "through faith and patience inherit the promises," which shows that patience is not a weakness but a weapon to persevere until the end. 2. It is also gentleness towards others: enduring without bitterness those who annoy or offend us. Ephesians 4:2 lists it as a virtue of the heart: "with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love." 3. Patience also appears as a stable consequence of faith: in 2 Timothy 3:10, Paul boasts of his "gentleness" (another translation of the same word), placing it alongside his teaching and faith. 4. Finally, it is God's great patience towards sinners. Romans 2:4 speaks of "the goodness of God" and His "longsuffering" (that is, His great soul that tolerates for a long time), and Romans 9:22 shows God enduring with patience "the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction." God's patience is never indifference: it is an active mercy that gives time for repentance.
G3115.origine: The Greek word μακροθυμία comes from two elements: "makros" (long, great) and "thumos" (heart, soul, passion). It literally denotes a "great soul" or a "long soul" — the image is that of a soul large and powerful enough not to explode with anger or frustration. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates forms of the Hebrew root "אַף אָרֵךְ" ("aph arek"), literally "long nostril," a vivid image for a person who takes time before becoming inflamed. The word is related to "makrothymos" (patient, longsuffering) and stands in opposition to impatience and anger.
G3115.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the New Testament, particularly in the Pauline epistles (Romans, Corinthians, Galatians, Colossians, Timothy) and in the Catholic epistles (James, Peter). It designates sometimes a human virtue — that of the believer who must endure tribulations with steadfastness (Hebrews 6:12, James 5:10) — sometimes a fruit of the Holy Spirit in the Christian (Galatians 5:22, Colossians 3:12), and sometimes the major virtue of God. In God, it is linked to His goodness and aims at the repentance of the sinner: in Romans 9:22, God endures sinners "with much patience" before manifesting His wrath. Human patience thus imitates divine patience and reflects it.
G3115.portee: For the Christian, this entry reveals that patience is not a passive resignation, but a strength of character rooted in God. When Paul calls to imitate the ancients who "through faith and patience inherit the promises," he asserts that holding firm in trial is no less important than believing. It is also a weapon against impatience towards others: patiently enduring those who irritate us reflects the love and mercy of God Himself, who has been patient with us for so long. Finally, God's patience is a call to repentance: each day that passes without immediate punishment is an act of grace inviting the sinner to change their heart.

sens: In listening to or enduring something, without rushing or getting irritated
With calm and kind firmness in the face of what requires time or understanding
G3116.detail:
1. The word describes the manner of listening to or enduring something: without impatience, without anger, taking the necessary time. Paul asks King Agrippa to listen to him "with patience" (Acts 26:3), meaning he requests calm and willing attention, despite the length or difficulty of what he is about to present. It is the adverb that accompanies the action, marking its measured and tranquil character.
2. The word also evokes moral firmness: enduring with calmness and kindness. It means not allowing oneself to be irritated, not immediately rejecting what is presented to us, but giving the speaker the time and attention they deserve.
G3116.origine: The word comes from "makros" (long, great) and "thumos" (passion, anger). The image is that of a soul that remains large, vast, that does not shrink under the effect of passion. It is a patience that does not wear out, a longsuffering. The related noun "makrothymia" (patience, longsuffering) appears several times in the Pauline epistles to describe a virtue of the Christian heart.
G3116.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 26:3, in adverbial form. It is Paul in chains asking King Agrippa to listen to him. The context is that of a defense before a sovereign: Paul does not ask for a favorable judgment, but to be heard with serenity, without bias. The adverb thus qualifies the mode of listening that Paul appeals to: a calm and equitable attention.
G3116.portee: This word reminds the reader that true listening — the kind that can lead to faith — requires patience. It is a virtue often forgotten: taking the time to truly hear, without impatience or prejudice, is an act of respect towards the speaker and the truth they bear.

sens: that extends over a great distance or duration
that is located at a great distance, far away
G3117.detail:
1. The word first designates what occupies a lot of space or time: in Mark 12:40 and Luke 20:47, it qualifies the "long" prayers that the Pharisees make "for appearance" — prayers that stretch out, that drag on.
2. It then designates what is distant, located far away: in Luke 15:13, the prodigal son goes to a "distant country" (literally: a far country, which is not near), just as in Luke 19:12 the nobleman goes to a "far country" to receive royal authority. The meaning shifts from "long" spatially to "distant," to "that is far from here."
G3117.origine: The word μακρός comes from an ancient Greek root associated with the idea of "greatness" and "extent." It translates in the Greek Old Testament the Hebrew words אָרֹךְ ("length") and רָחוֹק ("distant"), which share the same image: something that occupies space, that extends, and thus is far or lasts. The family of the word includes other terms that express distance or extent.
G3117.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the Gospel according to Luke and Mark, always in the first three Gospels. It is first used to qualify the long hypocritical prayers of the Pharisees (Mark 12:40 and Luke 20:47): these prayers are long only to appear, not to be true. It is then used to describe the distance of a country (Luke 15:13 and 19:12): the "distant" or "far" country emphasizes the physical and symbolic distance of the prodigal son from his father, or the nobleman's long journey before returning.
G3117.portee: This word helps us see how the Gospel critiques religious appearance: the long prayers of the Pharisees lack sincerity. It also reminds us that distance — that of the prodigal son who went far from his father — illustrates the estrangement of sin, which only return and forgiveness can bridge. The "length" and the "distance" become images of rupture and reconciliation.

sens: To have a long lifespan
To enjoy an extended existence on earth
G3118.detail:
1. The word describes someone who lives long, who has a life of great duration. It conveys the idea of an existence stretched over time, without premature end. In Ephesians 6:3, Paul cites the commandment from the Decalogue: "that it may go well with you and that you may live long on the earth," a promise of longevity attached to honoring parents.

2. Figuratively, it also evokes a fruitful and beneficial life, not just long but full. The biblical promise does not only guarantee numerous years, but happy and stable years.
G3118.origine: The word is composed of two Greek elements: makros ("long, great") and chronos ("time, duration"). The basic image is that of time extending, of a prolonged period. In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses the expression "to lengthen days" (אָרַךְ יוֹמִים) to express the same idea. The Septuagint (an ancient Greek translation) often renders this Hebrew notion with makrochronios or the expression makros ginetai, showing how both languages express the same biblical concept of blessed longevity.
G3118.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Ephesians 6:3. Paul uses it while quoting the fifth commandment from Exodus and Deuteronomy: honoring father and mother is the first commandment with a promise — that of living long. This word exactly captures the notion from the Old Testament, where long life is the promised blessing for faithful children. Its use shows that Paul connects the New Testament to the Old Covenant and sees the promise of longevity as still valid.
G3118.portee: This promise reminds believers that obedience is not a hollow burden, but carries with it concrete blessings. Honoring one's parents is not an abstract obligation: it is a path to a happy life and a stable existence on earth. The word invites us to take seriously that Christian morality is linked to our real well-being and to see God's commandments not as constraints, but as guardians of our life.

sens: Weakness or weakening of the body
State of illness or physical incapacity
Lack of vigor or strength
Powerlessness or insufficiency
G3119.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a physical weakness, a softness or lack of tone in the body — this is the initial image of the Greek word. In Matthew 4:23, Jesus heals "every disease and every infirmity": these are states of poor health that weaken the person and deprive them of their strength.

2. More broadly, infirmity is any state of illness or incapacity that prevents the body from functioning normally. It can be temporary or lasting, visible or hidden. Jesus gives his disciples "the power to heal every disease and every infirmity" (Matthew 10:1), showing that it opposes health and life in their fullness.

3. The word can also express a form of powerlessness or general insufficiency — not only physical but also moral or spiritual: it is the lack of what is necessary to act or to be complete.
G3119.origine: The Greek word comes from an adjective (malakos) meaning "soft, tender, weak." In classical Greek, it denoted softness or effeminacy. In the Greek Bible (Septuagint), it translates the Hebrew word for "disease" (choli), and gradually took on the more specific meaning of "physical weakness" or "infirmity." In the New Testament, it closely approaches the word ἀσθένεια (asthéneia), which also means "weakness."
G3119.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, all in the Gospel of Matthew, in the same three verses (4:23, 9:35, 10:1). Each time, it is paired with "disease" and describes the state of the people whom Jesus comes to heal. Infirmity is what renders the people helpless, sick, unable to live fully. It is an act of compassion from Jesus to heal it, and a proof of his power to grant it to his disciples.
G3119.portee: For the believer, understanding infirmity at the heart of Jesus' mission reminds us that the Gospel is addressed to the weak, the sick, the vulnerable. Jesus did not come for the healthy, but for those who suffer and lack. This also invites the disciple to see compassion and healing as signs of the Kingdom of God in action.

sens: Tender, soft to the touch (opposite of hard)
Garment, fabric, or precious delicate clothing
Gentle character, meekness, soft way of living
Softness, effeminacy
G3120.detail:
1. The word primarily describes what is tender and soft to the touch — a fine fabric, sensitive flesh, the opposite of a hard or rough surface. This is the basic concrete image: one feels the softness of the fabric against the skin.

2. The Bible mainly uses it for precious clothing: "those who wear fine clothes are in kings' houses" (Matthew 11:8, Luke 7:25). Silk or fine linen robes, worn by the rich and noble, are soft and delicate — a luxury that only the powerful can afford.

3. The word can also evoke a gentle temperament, meekness, a way of living that is soft and delicate, oriented towards comfort and pleasures. It is the character of one who is not accustomed to difficulties.

4. In 1 Corinthians 6:9, Paul uses it (probably in an obscene sense) to describe a form of effeminacy or moral softness — the absence of virility or spiritual strength. Here it represents the pejorative pole of the word: not virtuous softness, but culpable weakness.
G3120.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "soft" or "tender." In Hebrew, the Old Testament Greek renders it by רַךְ (rakh, "tender," "soft") in Proverbs 25:15, where a tender word breaks the bone — the image of what yields, what bends. The word also has a well-attested Greek family: it is applied to skin, fabrics, and people without resilience.
G3120.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament. The first two uses (Matthew 11:8, Luke 7:25) are identical: Jesus mentions the precious and soft clothing worn in kings' palaces, to show that John the Baptist, on the other hand, lived in the desert, as an ascetic. The context is one of wealth and comfort. The third use (1 Corinthians 6:9) places it in a list of serious sins, with a probable sexual connotation: it is the effeminacy condemned as incompatible with the Kingdom. The meaning shifts from the physical (soft fabric) to the moral (soft character, weakness) and to the spiritual (absence of moral strength in the face of evil).
G3120.portee: This word reveals how the Bible views softness: it can be a sign of comfort and wealth (which are not inherently bad), but it can also become a softness that renders us incapable of resisting sin. For the Christian, the issue is not to reject comfort, but to avoid becoming weak, soft, defenseless in the face of temptations and challenges of faith.

sens: Ancestor of Jesus in the genealogy of Luke, living before the Flood
G3121.detail: Mahalalel is an antediluvian patriarch mentioned only once in Luke 3:37. He appears in the genealogy that Luke traces back to Adam to show that Jesus is part of the entire history of salvation since creation. Son of Kenan and father of Methuselah, he represents a link in the unbroken chain that connects Adam to Jesus through the ages.
G3121.origine: The Hebrew name מַהֲלַלְאֵל (Mahalalel) literally means "praise of God" or "God gives praise," composed of the verb "to praise" and the noun "God." This name reflects the piety of the antediluvian patriarchs and their recognition of the Creator. Luke retains this name in its Greek form to honor the transmission of faith through generations.
G3121.emploi: Mahalalel appears only once in Luke 3:37, in the genealogy of Christ. He is a character from the primordial narrative reported in Genesis 5:12-17, where he is presented as one of the sons of God who walked with God like his father Enoch. Luke includes him in his ancestry of the Messiah to show that Jesus descends from a blessed and faithful lineage, since the origins of humanity.
G3121.portee: Mahalalel reminds us that Jesus does not arrive in history as an isolated figure, but that he is part of a divine plan that spans the centuries. His inclusion in the genealogy underscores the continuity of the divine promise and faithful faith: even before the Law given to Moses, there were men who walked with God and praised Him.

sens: What deserves the most attention, what comes first
What surpasses everything else in importance or degree
What particularly concerns a group or category
G3122.detail: 1. The word designates what is primary, what matters above all in a given situation: when Paul says that the Ephesians "embraced him, especially grieved because of what he had said that they would see his face no more" (Acts 20:38), it is this separation that occupies the heart most completely. 2. It expresses the highest degree, where something surpasses everything else: "We put our hope in the living God, who is the Savior of all men, especially of believers" (1 Timothy 4:10) means that God saves everyone, but believers benefit from a more complete salvation. 3. It marks a priority or particular preference within a whole: "Let us do good to all, and especially to those who are of the household of faith" (Galatians 6:10) indicates that everyone deserves our help, but the brothers in faith require special attention.
G3122.origine: The word comes from the root μάλα (mála), which means "very, much" — the adjective expressing the superlative of this intensity. The form μάλιστα is the superlative: it concentrates the idea of intensity to its maximum point. It can appear in the positive (very), comparative (more), and superlative (most, especially) forms depending on the context.
G3122.emploi: The word μάλιστα is very frequent in the New Testament, especially in Paul and Peter's writings. It regularly marks a priority or particular intensity. Acts 20:38 and 25:26 use it to indicate what occupies the heart or deserves primary attention. In 1 Timothy 4:10, 5:8, and 5:17, as well as in Galatians 6:10, it directs the reader towards a responsibility or obligation that takes precedence: towards believers, family, elders. Philippians 4:22 uses it for the saints of Caesar's household. Its constant use emphasizes a logic of gradation: not an exclusion of others, but a graduated attention.
G3122.portee: This word teaches a practical principle: charity and responsibility are not indifferent; they have concentric circles. The Christian must help all men, but his brothers and family require a more ardent expectation. This does not contradict universal love but concretizes it: one loves first those close to oneself, according to one's most immediate duties, before opening up to all humanity.

sens: More, in greater quantity or intensity
In a superior manner, with more strength or value
Rather, by preference, by choice
Always more, continually increased
G3123G.detail:
1. The simplest meaning: an increased quantity or intensity. "Your birds of the air do not sow, nor reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they?" (Matthew 6:26). You have greater value.
2. A superiority or excellence: what is better, stronger, more glorious. "The ministry of righteousness is much more glorious" than that of condemnation (2 Corinthians 3:9). This means: it surpasses, it prevails.
3. Choice, preference, voluntary orientation: "rather" than, "preferably". It expresses what one prefers. The Apostle Paul says: "I would rather depart and be with Christ" (Philippians 1:23) — he chooses this rather than present life.
4. Continuous progression, repeated growth: "more and more". "The fame of Jesus spread more and more, and great multitudes came together" (Luke 5:15). An endless increase, a multiplication.
G3123G.origine: The Greek word μᾶλλον comes from the root μάλα, which means "very, much". It is the comparative form: "more much" becomes "more". In Hebrew, it often translates the particle מ (min), which marks comparison and surplus. This word expresses the idea of surpassing, of progressive increase — it carries the image of weight being added to weight, of quantity increasing.
G3123G.emploi: This word appears fifty times in the New Testament, especially in Paul and the Gospels. It functions in three main ways. First, it measures a superior quantity or intensity: "much more" (Matthew 6:26, Romans 5:15). Then, it compares two things and establishes a hierarchy: "the ministry of righteousness is much more glorious" (2 Corinthians 3:9). Finally, it expresses a choice, a conscious preference: "rather" accept an injustice than resort to courts (1 Corinthians 9:12), or "desire rather" to depart with Christ (Philippians 1:23). It can also mark continuous growth: "the fame spread more and more" (Luke 5:15), "you were increasingly added to" (Acts 5:14).
G3123G.portee: This word invites the reader to weigh values: who really matters? what deserves to be preferred? It pushes to see beyond the visible: you are more valuable than the birds (Matthew 6:26), grace surpasses condemnation (2 Corinthians 3:9). It also helps to understand God's logic: if He did this for the unbelievers, how much more for His children. It is a word that calls to grow, to advance, to choose what is better.

sens: more, more intensely
more, in greater measure (comparative)
preferably, rather than something else
G3123H.detail:
1. The word expresses an increase, an intensification: "more". When it is said that something is done "more" or "rather", it emphasizes that it is progressing, growing. For example, the Word was spreading and the number of disciples was growing "more" (Acts 5:14 in the source definition).

2. It is a word of comparison between two states or two quantities: one is "more" than the other. This comparison can relate to an action, a quality, or a number. For example, it is better (it is more good) that a millstone be hung around your neck than to offend one of these little ones (Mark 9:42).

3. The word expresses a conscious choice: one prefers one thing over another, choosing it "rather" than its opposite. It is an act of will. Thus, Peter and the apostles declare: "We ought to obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29) — they reject human order to obey God.
G3123H.origine: The word comes from an ancient Greek adjective meaning "very, much". It is a comparative (a form that expresses comparison): it stands between the ordinary positive and the superlative (the highest degree). The root evokes intensity, increase. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates Hebrew or Aramaic particles marking comparison or preference (like מ in Hebrew), which shows that it has retained this meaning across both Testaments.
G3123H.emploi: The word appears 31 times in the New Testament. It is mainly used in Pauline epistles and in the Gospels. Used alone, it means "more, rather" (Acts 5:14). Strengthened by an adjective ("much more", "well more"), it emphasizes the intensity of a comparison: "are you not much more" than the birds (Matthew 6:26 in the source definition). Placed after a verb of preference or will, it expresses choice: "I prefer", "I would rather" (1 Corinthians 14:5). It can also oppose two realities: "rather than" or "rather some... than...". In moral exhortations, it guides towards good: rather forgiveness (2 Corinthians 2:7), rather thanksgiving (Ephesians 5:4).
G3123H.portee: For the Christian reader, this word invites discernment of priorities. When Paul says "rather obey God than men" or "rather suffer injustice than commit it", he calls the believer to prioritize his choices: to put God first, to prefer justice and love over comfort. It is a word of moral decision: it is not enough to do good; one must also consciously prefer it over what contradicts it.

sens: servant of the high priest in Jerusalem
G3124.detail: Malchus is the servant (or slave) of the high priest who likely accompanied the group sent to arrest Jesus on the night from Thursday to Friday of the trial (John 18:10). He is the one whose right ear Simon Peter cuts off in the Garden of Gethsemane at the moment of Jesus' arrest.
G3124.origine: The Greek name Malchus is the Hellenized form of the Hebrew word melekh (מֶלֶךְ), which literally means "king." It is a name borne by servants in the ancient Mediterranean world, likely chosen here simply as a proper name without relation to its etymological meaning.
G3124.emploi: Malchus appears only once in the New Testament, in John 18:10. He is mentioned solely to identify the servant whose ear was cut off during the arrest of Jesus. This is a concrete and vivid detail that only John reports in his Gospel, revealing his eyewitness source and compassion for all characters, including minor actors.

sens: Grandmother, the mother of the mother or father
G3125.detail: 1. The word refers to the mother of the parents, the generation preceding that of the parents. In 2 Timothy 1:5, Paul speaks of Lois, Timothy's grandmother, who had a sincere faith that was passed down to her mother Eunice, and then to Timothy himself. It is a simple and tender word, one that a child would naturally use to talk about their grandmother.
G3125.origine: The word μάμμη is an onomatopoeia, that is, a word imitated from the babble of children (like "mama"). Originally, in classical Greek, it affectionately referred to the mother. Later, during the New Testament period, it came to also mean grandmother, taking on the usage of the ancient Greek word τήθη. It is a familiar word, from everyday language and tender.
G3125.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 1:5. Paul mentions Lois, Timothy's grandmother, to remind his young collaborator that the faith he possesses comes from a family transmission: it first dwelled in Lois, then in his mother Eunice, before filling Timothy himself. This passage shows how genuine faith can traverse generations of a family.
G3125.portee: This word emphasizes the strength of faith transmission through family ties. The fact that Paul reminds Timothy of his grandmother's name and faith shows that spiritual roots matter and that the prayer and example of previous generations bear fruit. It is an encouragement for Christians to cultivate a living faith that they can pass on to their children.

sens: the money and material possessions owned
the financial resources of a person or community
what attracts human love and desire
what can become a competing master to God in a person's heart
G3126.detail:
1. The word concretely refers to money, gold, and all material goods one possesses. It is a person's fortune, their assets. Jesus speaks of "unjust riches" (Luke 16:9, 16:11), meaning those obtained dishonestly or misused.
2. More broadly, it encompasses all financial resources available to someone — their money, their ability to pay, to buy, to possess. It is wealth as economic power.
3. The word also evokes what powerfully attracts humans: wealth becomes an object of desire, love, something that is coveted. This is why Jesus warns that "no one can serve two masters, one of those masters being mammon" (Matthew 6:24).
4. In Jesus' teaching, wealth becomes a rival spiritual force, almost personified as a god, capable of turning a person's heart away from God Himself. It is a trap: one cannot love God and wealth with the same intensity.
G3126.origine: The word comes from the Aramaic מָמוֺנָא (mamona), which literally means "wealth" or "that in which one puts their trust." Aramaic was the language spoken in Palestine at the time of Jesus. This word was introduced into Greek exactly as it was spoken — without translation, as a loanword. It retains this foreign sound that makes it almost enigmatic, almost like a proper name. This underscores the particular nature of this wealth: it is not just money; it is a power, almost a divinity.
G3126.emploi: The word appears only 4 times in the New Testament, all occurrences found in the words of Jesus: twice in Matthew (6:24) and three times in Luke (16:9, 16:11, 16:13). Jesus uses it to teach about the spiritual danger of the love of money. In the passages from chapter 16 of Luke (the parable of the unjust steward), Jesus calls wealth "unjust" to show that it is often tainted by injustice or diverts from justice. In Matthew 6:24, Jesus says that one cannot "serve" two masters — this verb "serve" personifies wealth as a rival god.
G3126.portee: This word challenges the Christian regarding their relationship to money and material goods. Jesus does not condemn wealth in itself, but the love of wealth: it is this love that becomes idolatry, a worship rendered to a false god. For the disciple, it is a call to examine their heart: to whom or to what am I truly faithful? It also invites a redefinition of wealth: Jesus speaks of making "friends with unjust riches" (Luke 16:9), meaning to use money for the good of others and not for oneself.

sens: man who grew up in the court of Herod Antipas
G3127.detail: Manahen is a prophet and teacher of the early church in Antioch, mentioned only once in the Acts. The text specifies that he had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch (Acts 13:1), meaning he grew up in the court of the Jewish prince who ruled over Galilee. His appearance in the list of the early spiritual leaders of Antioch suggests that he had become a recognized leader of the young Christian community, despite his past in the circles of political and worldly power.
G3127.origine: The name Manahen comes from the Hebrew Menahem (מְנַחֵם), which means "the one who comforts" or "comforter." It is a Hebrew name borne by other important figures in Jewish history, including a king of Israel. The name reflects the Jewish heritage of this character and his culture of origin.
G3127.emploi: Manahen appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 13:1, where Luke presents him as one of the five prophets and teachers of the church in Antioch at the time when the Holy Spirit calls them to missionary service. His inclusion in this group of spiritual leaders, alongside Barnabas and Saul (who will become the apostle Paul), indicates that he played an active role in the ministry of this influential community. His personal journey — having been at the court of a Jewish king, then converted and integrated into Christian leadership — shows how the Christian movement attracted men from all social backgrounds, including those who had access to the upper echelons of Palestinian society.
G3127.portee: The mention of Manahen reminds us that no one is too tied to the world or power to be transformed by the grace of God. His past in the entourage of Herod, a politically convenient king with the Romans, did not prevent him from becoming a prophet and teacher in the nascent church. His story invites the reader to see that God calls people from all walks of life and places them in positions of responsibility according to His Spirit, regardless of their status or past.

sens: Eldest son of Joseph and his wife Asenath
Tribe of Israel descended from this son
King of Judah in the 7th century B.C.
G3128G.detail: 1. Manasseh is the eldest son of Joseph, who acknowledges him as his own in Egypt despite his birth before the official marriage to Asenath. It is a name that means in Hebrew "the one who makes forget," for Joseph says in naming him that God has made him forget his sorrow and his father's house (Genesis 41:51). 2. The tribe of Manasseh gathers the descendants of this son and becomes one of the twelve tribes of Israel. This tribe receives its inheritance in the promised land, first east of the Jordan (Gilead) and then also to the west. In Revelation 7:6, it is listed among the tribes sealed by God, with twelve thousand chosen from each tribe. 3. A king bearing this name reigns over the kingdom of Judah in the 7th century; he is the son of Hezekiah. Matthew mentions him in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:10).
G3128G.origine: The name Manasseh comes from the Hebrew מְנַשֶּׁה (Menashé), derived from a root meaning "to forget, to make forget." This name reflects the etymology given by the biblical text itself: Joseph declares that God has made him forget his suffering. The name designates both a historical person and a tribe, as is common in the Bible where ancestors found the peoples that bear their name.
G3128G.emploi: The name Manasseh primarily designates Joseph's son in Egypt, recognized by Jacob and integrated into the lineage of the patriarchs despite his mixed origins (Egyptian mother). This creates two half-tribes called Ephraim and Manasseh, which replace the name of Joseph in the division of the promised land. The tribe of Manasseh becomes one of the most important in the northern kingdom. Later, a king of Judah bears this name; he reigns for a long time and first experiences trial (captivity in Assyria) before repenting and restoring worship. In Revelation 7:6, the tribe of Manasseh is among those marked with the divine seal, a sign of protection and belonging to God in times of distress.
G3128G.portee: Manasseh embodies forgiveness and restoration: despite ambiguous origins and a history of disobedience (for the king), the name persists in Scripture and among the people of Israel. Its appearance in Revelation 7 reminds us that even in the final judgment, the twelve tribes — figures of the Israel of Salvation — receive divine protection. The Christian can see in this the reflection of God's infinite forgiveness towards the one who repents.

sens: Eldest son of Joseph and his Egyptian mother Asenath
Tribe of Israel descended from this son
King of Judah in the 7th century B.C.
G3128H.detail: 1. Manasseh is the eldest son that Joseph had with Asenath, the Egyptian woman given to him by Pharaoh. Although he is the firstborn, he was placed after his younger brother Ephraim in Jacob's blessing (Genesis 48), symbolizing that God does not always follow the natural order. 2. The tribe of Manasseh, derived from his name, became one of the twelve tribes of Israel and occupied a region in the Promised Land. Revelation mentions this tribe among the children of Israel on the day of judgment (Revelation 7:6). 3. Manasseh was king of Judah in the 7th century B.C.; the Gospel of Matthew mentions him in the genealogy of Jesus, between Hezekiah and Amon (Matthew 1:10).
G3128H.origine: The Hebrew name מְנַשֶּׁה (Menashshé) literally means "the one who makes forget." Joseph explained it this way: "God has made me forget all my trouble and all my father's household" (Genesis 41:51). This name expresses divine grace that erases painful memories and uprooting.
G3128H.emploi: Manasseh designates three biblical realities: Joseph's son, the tribe of Israel that descends from him, and the king of Judah. In the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:10), he appears as king of Judah, a link in the chain that connects Abraham to Christ according to the promise. The word also appears in Revelation (7:6) to enumerate the tribes of Israel on the day of divine judgment.
G3128H.portee: The name Manasseh reminds us that God forgives and erases the wounds of the past. His presence in the genealogy of Christ shows that Jesus comes from a human royal lineage, and that the Messiah embraces the entire history of Israel, from the Promised Land to the kings who reign in Judea.

sens: to acquire knowledge, to understand something about a question
to receive teaching, to be formed through instruction
to discover, to become aware of a fact
to acquire a habit, to be formed through practice
G3129.detail:
1. To learn is primarily to understand something by informing oneself or studying. Paul tells the Corinthians: "Go and learn what this means: I desire mercy" (Matthew 9:13) — he invites them to grasp the meaning of a word. It is to acquire new knowledge by seeking to understand.
2. To learn also means to receive instruction from someone, to allow oneself to be formed. Jesus says: "Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart" (Matthew 11:29) — it is to put oneself in the school of someone, to listen in order to be transformed. In 1 Timothy 2:11, a woman must listen to "instruction in silence."
3. To learn can simply mean to observe, to discover a fact. The Roman commander "learned" that he was a Roman citizen (Acts 23:27) — he has just learned it, he has discovered it.
4. To learn is finally to acquire a habit through practice and experience. Paul says in Philippians 4:11: "I have learned to be content" — this was not innate, he acquired it through experience. It is to be formed in something progressively.
G3129.origine: The verb μανθάνω (manthanō) comes from an ancient root expressing the idea of "to grasp with the mind." In the Hebrew of the Old Testament (often translated by the word לָמַד, lamad), it also carries the idea of acquiring knowledge through study and discipline. The family of the word includes the noun μαθητής (mathétès), "disciple," one who learns — literally "the learner." This is why Jesus is called the master of the disciples: he is the one who forms them.
G3129.emploi: The verb "to learn" appears 24 times in the New Testament. It is found mainly in the epistles of Paul and in the Gospels. Sometimes it refers to learning a doctrine or a spiritual truth (Ephesians 4:20: "You did not learn Christ this way"; Romans 16:17: learning to avoid divisive people). Sometimes it involves learning a practice, an attitude (Philippians 4:11: learning contentment). Other times, it refers to receiving formal instruction (1 Timothy 2:11; 2 Timothy 3:14). Finally, to learn can simply mean "to discover" or "to hear about" (Acts 23:27). The meaning varies according to the context and what is learned.
G3129.portee: This verb reminds the Christian that faith is not given all at once, but is built through learning and formation. Following Jesus is not passive: it is to put oneself in his school, as a disciple learns from his master. Every believer remains a "learner" — he must learn the Scriptures, learn the attitudes of Christ, learn to live his faith. This word invites humility and discipline: becoming a Christian is to enter a school that lasts a lifetime.

G3130.fr: to be out of one's mind
sens: Loss of reason, madness
State of extreme agitation of the mind
Insensate speech or behavior
G3130.detail:
1. The word denotes a serious mental disturbance, a total or partial loss of control of reason. It is a state of madness where the mind is disordered. In Acts 26:24, Festus says to Paul, "You are out of your mind" upon hearing about the resurrection — for him, this faith was madness.
2. Concretely, it is a violent agitation of the mind, a form of derangement where the person loses self-control. The Greek word comes from the verb "to be out of oneself" and suggests an intense disturbance.
3. By extension, the word can qualify a speech or act that seems completely unreasonable to the one who hears it, even if the one speaking or acting is obeying a true conviction — this is what Paul experiences: the Roman authorities see his faith in the resurrection as pure folly.
G3130.origine: The word comes from the Greek μαίνομαι (maínomai), "to be out of oneself, to be in the grip of madness." This root evokes the image of someone whose mind is agitated, transported out of themselves. In the Greek Old Testament, the word translates the Hebrew מַשְׂטֵמָה (mastéma), which expresses hostility and confusion of the mind. The Greek root suggests a break from the normal order of rational thought.
G3130.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 26:24. Paul is on trial before Festus, a Roman governor, to justify himself against accusations. When Paul speaks of the resurrection of the dead and the appearance of the risen Christ, Festus abruptly interrupts him, saying that his great knowledge makes him "out of his mind" — in short, he judges the Christian faith as pure folly. This moment shows the contrast between the wisdom of the world (represented by Festus and Roman law) and the logic of the Gospel, which seems absurd to those who do not believe.
G3130.portee: This passage reminds us that faith in the risen Christ disturbs the wisdom of the world. In the eyes of human political and intellectual power, believing that God has risen from the dead may seem like madness. But Paul does not back down: he defends his conviction as a truth received directly from Christ. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation not to be ashamed of the Gospel, even if it clashes with human logic.

sens: Miraculous food sent by God to the people of Israel in the desert
Symbol of the bread of eternal life offered by Jesus
G3131.detail:
1. Manna is the miraculous bread that God gave daily to the Israelites during their forty years of wandering in the desert after the exodus from Egypt (Exodus 16). It resembled coriander seed and tasted like honey; every morning it covered the ground of the camp, and the people gathered it to eat. Jesus evokes this memory when he says, "Our fathers ate the manna in the desert" (John 6:31), but he also reminds that despite this divine food, the fathers "died" (John 6:49).
2. Jesus uses manna as an image of the eternal bread of life that he himself offers. When he declares, "whoever eats this bread will live forever" (John 6:58), he invites believers to move from earthly and temporal food to spiritual and eternal nourishment — himself, the true bread from heaven. In Revelation, the "hidden manna" promised to the victor symbolizes the spiritual rewards and divine mysteries reserved for those who persevere in faith (Revelation 2:17).
G3131.origine: The word manna comes from the Hebrew man, which literally means "what is it?" — the very name that the Israelites asked themselves upon seeing this unknown substance every morning in the desert. In Hebrew, they would say "man hu?" (what is it?), and this curious name has remained. The Greek text uses the word manna as is, as it was the traditional name passed down by Jewish tradition. This word recalls the astonishment and mystery before God's action.
G3131.emploi: The word manna appears five times in the New Testament, exclusively to refer to this desert food or its spiritual meaning. The three occurrences in John 6 (verses 31, 49, 58) are part of the great discourse on the bread of life: Jesus contrasts the old manna, which nourished the body but left the eaters dead, with himself, who offers eternal life. An occurrence in Hebrews 9:4 mentions the manna kept in a golden jar inside the Ark of the Covenant, symbolizing Israel's most sacred treasure. Finally, Revelation 2:17 speaks of the "hidden manna" as a promised reward to the one who overcomes, transposing the gift from the desert into an eschatological promise — what will be given in heaven to the victors.
G3131.portee: Meditating on manna invites the believer to see in Jesus the true bread that came down from heaven, superior to any earthly or legal food. It reminds that faith in Christ, unlike the old observances, gives a life that does not end with death: it is the transition from the Old Testament to the reality it foreshadowed. For those who suffer or struggle to maintain their trust in God, manna is a sign that God provides for our needs each day, just as he did for Israel.

sens: To predict the future or know the occult through magical arts or demonic practices
To practice divination or magic claiming a false supernatural power
G3132.detail:
1. The verb means to know or announce the future through magic, witchcraft, or contact with spirits: a slave girl possessed by a "spirit of Python" (a demonic spirit believed to give prophetic powers) divined the future for her masters, who profited from it (Acts 16:16). This is false prophecy, opposed to the true word of God.
2. The word designates the whole range of occult practices — divination by entrails, by dreams, consulting spirits — that pagan peoples used to seek to know the future or hidden secrets. It is a human art without God, rejected by the Law (Deuteronomy 18:10).
G3132.origine: The word comes from μαντίς (mantis), which means "diviner" or "seer" — one who claims to see what is hidden. In Hebrew, this verb translates קָסַם (qasam), "to practice divination," a word of the same root as "diviner" in French. The Greek family also includes the word for the type of divination: μαντεία (manteia), "divination." This is never true prophecy inspired by God (προφητεύω), but always a false human or demonic imitation.
G3132.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Greek New Testament (Acts 16:16). Paul and Silas encounter a slave girl who "divined" to earn money for her masters. She was possessed by a demonic spirit that allowed her, according to the pagan beliefs of Philippi, to predict the future. This context clearly identifies "to divine" as a magical practice linked to demonic possession and paganism, not to true divine prophecy.
G3132.portee: This word reminds us of the clear difference between the true and the false in the spiritual realm. True prophecy comes from God alone; one who "divines" seeks knowledge of the future outside of God, often through evil powers. For the believer, this passage invites rejection of occult curiosity — astrology, tarot, spiritism — and to trust in the living word of God rather than these seductive but deceptive imitations.

sens: To lose freshness and vigor, like a flower or plant that dries up
To decay, to weaken gradually
To disappear, to vanish (in a figurative sense)
G3133.detail:
1. The literal meaning is that of a plant that dries up: the grass and the flower lose their luster under the heat of the sun and eventually fall. This is the image that James uses in James 1:11: "The sun has risen with its scorching heat and has withered the grass; its flower has fallen, and the beauty of its appearance has vanished."
2. Figuratively, the word describes anything that weakens, consumes, or disappears: a beauty that fades, a strength that diminishes, a prosperity that declines. James applies it to the rich themselves: they "will wither in their pursuits," meaning that their wealth and prestige will not last, like the flower that falls under the sun.
G3133.origine: The word comes from a Greek root that evokes drying up and destruction. In Wisdom 2:8 and 19:21, it describes how transient things are destroyed or wear out. The Septuagint uses it to translate the Hebrew "yabesh" (יָבֵשׁ) in Job 15:30, which means "to dry" or "to wither." The word always evokes a loss of vitality and beauty.
