G3133.emploi: James is the only one to use this verb in the New Testament. He uses it to show the vanity of earthly wealth: the rich, like the flower under the scorching sun, cannot escape degradation and death. This striking image emphasizes that human prosperity is fleeting and lacks a stable foundation — a central theme of James' epistle on the insufficiency of riches.
G3133.portee: This word invites the believer not to place their trust in wealth or earthly advantages, which are by nature fleeting. Like the flower that withers, all human prosperity is fragile and temporary. James urges us to seek eternal wealth in Christ rather than an illusory security in material goods.

sens: Aramaic exclamation meaning "Lord, come!" or "The Lord comes"
G3134.detail: 1. This Aramaic expression, used as is by Paul without translation, is an invocation addressed to the Lord Jesus for Him to return. It expresses the passionate expectation and impatience of the early Christians regarding the imminent return of Christ. In 1 Corinthians 16:22, it appears as a heartfelt cry, a fervent prayer that seals Paul's letter: "If anyone does not love the Lord, let him be accursed. Maranatha."
G3134.origine: The expression is composed of two Aramaic words: "maran" (our Lord) and "atha" (comes). It retains the mother tongue of Jesus and the apostles, spoken in Galilee and Jerusalem. The fact that Paul reports it in Aramaic shows that it was a traditional liturgical word, likely used in early Christian assemblies, even in Greek-speaking communities. This expression bears witness to the Semitic roots of the nascent Christian worship.
G3134.emploi: The expression appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 16:22. Paul uses it at the end of his first letter to the Corinthians, immediately following a solemn word about love for the Lord. It occurs in a context of exhortation to faithfulness and expectation of eschatological judgment. By leaving it in Aramaic rather than translating it into Greek, Paul acknowledges its sacred and traditional character, showing that it was already well known among the early churches as a liturgical acclamation.
G3134.portee: "Maranatha" reminds the Christian that the return of the Lord is not an abstract doctrine but a living hope that should transform their attachment to Jesus and their way of living. This exclamation invites examination of one's love for the Lord (previous verse: "If anyone does not love the Lord") and to live in conscious anticipation of His coming. It expresses a fundamental biblical tension: Christ has already come, but has not yet returned, and believers must hold fast to this active hope.

sens: Precious gem produced by pearl oysters
A good of great material and commercial value
A symbol of something precious that should not be wasted
G3135.detail:
1. A pearl is a precious, shiny, and white stone produced naturally by the pearl oyster: it is the image of a rare and beautiful good, obtained at great cost. In the parable of Matthew 13:45-46, the merchant seeks fine pearls and sells all that he has to acquire a pearl of great price, representing the kingdom of heaven that the believer cherishes above all.
2. Pearls are among the most coveted luxury goods: they were worn as ornaments (1 Timothy 2:9), exchanged as precious merchandise (Revelation 18:12), and even adorned the heavenly Jerusalem (Revelation 21:21). They represent material wealth and splendor.
3. Figuratively, "casting pearls before swine" (Matthew 7:6) means offering what is precious to those who cannot appreciate it or will abuse it: it is about not wasting holy things on those who would despise them.
G3135.origine: The Greek word μαργαρίτης comes from the Mediterranean and Asian commercial world, where pearl farming was well established. It literally designates the pearl, this natural gem formed in the oyster. The word is probably of Indian or Persian origin, adopted by Greek to name this luxury good. It also appears in other Greek texts to evoke wealth and prestige.
G3135.emploi: The word pearl appears nine times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew and Revelation. In Matthew, it is used in the concrete sense (the ornaments of women) and in the figurative sense (the great value of the kingdom). In Revelation, pearls symbolize earthly wealth (as in the list of commercial cargoes of Babylon) and heavenly glory (the gates of the New Jerusalem made of pearls). In Paul, the word evokes excess luxury to be avoided. The context varies: sometimes it is a good to be coveted and purchased at great cost, sometimes an ornament of vanity, sometimes an image of inestimable value.
G3135.portee: Understanding the word "pearl" in the Bible helps the believer to measure the infinite value of the kingdom of God: like the merchant in the parable, he must be willing to abandon everything that restricts him to serve it. It is also an invitation not to profane holy things by offering them to those who would reject them. Finally, this word reminds us that beauty and value, in the Bible, do not reside in earthly ornaments, but in what is eternal.

sens: woman from Bethany, sister of Mary and Lazarus
G3136.detail: Martha is a woman who lived in the village of Bethany, near Jerusalem. She appears in the Gospels as the sister of Mary and Lazarus, three close friends of Jesus. Luke first shows her welcoming Jesus into her home (Luke 10:38), but absorbed in the cares of service to the point of forgetting her inner peace — the Lord gently tells her: "Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things" (Luke 10:41). John then presents her during the death of her brother Lazarus: she runs to meet Jesus with a firm heart, confessing her faith in the resurrection (John 11:20-24), and then she asks Jesus to remove the stone from the tomb before he raises him (John 11:39).
G3136.origine: The name Martha comes from Aramaic and means "mistress" or "lady" — it expresses an idea of responsibility and leadership. It is a common woman's name in first-century Judaism.
G3136.emploi: Martha appears twelve times in the New Testament, only in the Gospel of Luke and in that of John. Luke stages her during a visit from Jesus to her home, where she contrasts with her sister Mary, who sits at the Lord's feet to listen to him. John recounts her story at length during the death and resurrection of Lazarus, where she plays a role of trust and dialogue with Jesus. The two portraits complement each other: an active woman, committed to concrete service, but also capable of deep faith in the power and compassion of the Lord.
G3136.portee: Martha speaks to every believer: she shows how the busyness of service, even for a good cause, can distance us from what is essential — the personal relationship with Jesus. But she also teaches that practical love and hospitality are not to be despised in themselves. Her dialogue with Jesus at the time of Lazarus's death invites us to cultivate a living faith, to believe that the Lord hears our prayers and can intervene even in the face of the impossible.

sens: Mother of Jesus
Mary Magdalene, converted sinner
Wife of Clopas, mother of James the Less
Sister of Martha and Lazarus
Mother of John Mark
Christian greeted by Paul
G3137G.detail:
1. Mary, the mother of Jesus, is the woman who conceived and gave birth to the promised Messiah. She is betrothed to Joseph, a carpenter from Nazareth, and it is after the announcement of the angel Gabriel that she receives the word of God in faith (Luke 1:27, 1:38). She accompanies Jesus to Jerusalem, witnesses his crucifixion, and is among the first disciples after the resurrection (John 19:25, Acts 1:14).
2. Mary Magdalene is a woman converted from a life of sin (John 11:2, 12:3), who becomes a faithful disciple following Jesus and staying with him until the cross.
3. Mary, wife of Clopas, is the mother of James the Less and Joses. She is among the women present at the crucifixion and the resurrection (Matthew 27:56, 27:61, 28:1).
4. Mary, sister of Martha and Lazarus, is the one who sits at Jesus' feet to listen to him teach, an image of the attitude of a true disciple (Luke 10:39, 10:42).
5. Mary, mother of John Mark, welcomes the apostles into her home in Jerusalem, a place of gathering and prayer for the early Church (Acts 12:12).
6. A Christian in Rome to whom the apostle Paul sends his personal greetings, recognizing her service to the saints (Romans 16:6).
G3137G.origine: The Greek name Μαρία (Maria) is a Hellenization of the Aramaic name Μαριάμ (Mariam) and the Hebrew מִרְיָם (Miriam). It is related to the name of the prophetess Miriam, sister of Moses in the Old Testament. The original meaning of the name is uncertain, but it has marked the history of all Jewish peoples in antiquity.
G3137G.emploi: The name Mary appears 26 times in the New Testament, referring to six different women from the apostolic era. The most mentioned is Mary, the mother of Jesus, present from the Annunciation (Luke 1:27-1:39), throughout the public life (Matthew 13:55, Mark 6:3), at the cross (John 19:25), and among the apostles after the Ascension (Acts 1:14). She meditates on the words and actions of Jesus (Luke 2:19) and receives the prophetic announcement of the suffering that will pierce her soul (Luke 2:34). The other Marys are women of faith who support Jesus and the service of the Church: the women at the tomb at the resurrection (Matthew 28:1), the contemplative disciple who listens to the Word (Luke 10:39), and the Christian women who serve the Assembly.
G3137G.portee: Mary, the mother of Jesus, is the model of welcoming faith: she says "yes" to God's call despite her confusion and fear (Luke 1:38). Her life teaches how to keep the Word deep in the heart and meditate on it (Luke 2:19). The other Marys show various forms of Christian service: listening to the Word, faithfulness to the cross, and hospitality towards the Church. Together, these portraits of faithful women remind us that the Lord works through ordinary human instruments, often women, and that faith is proven through obedience and persevering service.

sens: Mother of Jesus
Mary of Magdala
Wife of Clopas, mother of James and Joses
Sister of Martha and Lazarus
Mother of John Mark
Christian greeted by Paul
G3137I.detail:
1. Mother of Jesus, the one who conceived and gave birth to the Messiah. She appears in the infancy narratives and remains in Jerusalem after the Ascension, praying with the apostles (Acts 1:14).
2. Woman of Magdala, who followed Jesus and was healed by him. She is the first to see the risen Lord and runs to announce it to the disciples (John 20:1, 16, 18).
3. Wife of Clopas, present at the foot of the cross. She is the mother of James the Less and Joses, and she comes to see the tomb on the morning of the resurrection with other women (Matthew 27:56, 61; 28:1).
4. Sister of Martha and the resurrected Lazarus. She sits at Jesus' feet to listen to his teaching and anoints him with perfume before his passion (Luke 10:39; John 11:1-2; 12:3).
5. Mother of John Mark, who opens her home to the Jerusalem assembly for prayer (Acts 12:12).
6. Woman of the assembly in Rome, known to Paul for her work in the Lord (Romans 16:6).
G3137I.origine: The name comes from the Aramaic מַרְיָם (Miryam). Its exact meaning remains debated, but it could be related to the Hebrew מֶרֶם (height) or to a root meaning "bitter" or "beloved." It is a name also borne in the Old Testament, notably by the sister of Moses. Greek uses two forms: Μαρία (Maria), the usual Hellenized form, and Μαριάμ (Mariam), a form closer to the original Aramaic.
G3137I.emploi: The name Mary designates at least six women in the New Testament, showing how common this name was in Israel. The best known is Mary of Magdala, who appears at key moments in the ministry and resurrection of Jesus: she accompanies him, receives healing, remains at the foot of the cross (John 19:25), and is the first to meet the Risen One on the morning of the first day (John 20:1, 11, 16, 18). Mary, mother of Jesus, is mentioned mainly in the Lord's infancy and once after his resurrection (Acts 1:14), confirming her presence in the early community. The other Marys (the one of Clopas, the one of Magdala according to some accounts, the one of Martha) appear less often but play important roles as witnesses of the cross and resurrection, or as close disciples of the Lord.
G3137I.portee: The women named Mary illustrate the importance of women in the history of salvation and in the Christian assembly. They are witnesses to decisive moments: the birth of the Messiah, his passion, his resurrection. Mary of Magdala, freed from seven demons and the first to see the Risen One, shows that women's faith is not lesser and that Jesus honors them. The narrative also emphasizes that discipleship is not reserved for men: the women named Mary follow, serve, worship, and testify with remarkable authenticity and faithfulness.

sens: Sister of Martha and Lazarus, from Bethany
G3137J.detail: Mary of Bethany is the younger sister of Martha and the sister of Lazarus. She lived in the village of Bethany, near Jerusalem, and appears in the Gospel of John and that of Luke as a woman who chooses to listen to Jesus rather than concern herself with household tasks (Luke 10:39-42). She is also the one who anointed Jesus' feet with expensive perfume and wiped them with her hair, an act of devotion and worship towards the Lord (John 11:2, John 12:3). When her brother Lazarus fell seriously ill, she remained seated at home while her sister Martha went to meet Jesus; this distinction of character between the two sisters illustrates two ways of living faith.
G3137J.origine: Mary comes from the Greek Maria (Hellenized) and Mariam (Aramaic מַרְיָם), a form that also appears in Hebrew מִרְיָם. The name was common in first-century Judaism and has several bearers in the New Testament: the mother of Jesus, Mary Magdalene, the wife of Clopas, and this Mary of Bethany, the closest companion of Jesus in Judea with her family.
G3137J.emploi: Mary of Bethany appears in the Gospel of John (chapters 11 and 12) and is mentioned once in the Gospel of Luke (10:39-42). Luke depicts her in her home where she sits at Jesus' feet to listen, while Martha is busy serving: Jesus declares that Mary "has chosen the good part." John primarily presents her as the one who anointed Jesus with perfume during a meal in Bethany six days before Passover (John 12:3), an act of worship and personal devotion. She also appears alongside Martha during Lazarus' illness and resurrection, where she shows her love for the Lord by coming to throw herself at his feet in tears (John 11:32). Her biblical portrait reveals a contemplative soul, attached to the presence and teaching of Christ.
G3137J.portee: Mary of Bethany teaches the reader the importance of cultivating a personal intimacy with Jesus through listening to His word and worship. Her choice to listen rather than to be distracted by activities, even pious ones, shows that communion with Christ surpasses external works. Her act of anointing Jesus with perfume also foreshadows the sincere love that recognizes Him as Lord and Master, a model of living faith and personal devotion. She invites every believer to seek first what lasts: to know Jesus rather than to be absorbed by the tumult of concerns.

sens: Jewish woman of the first century, wife of Clopas
mother of James the Less and Joses
faithful disciple present at the crucifixion and resurrection of the Lord
G3137K.detail:
1. Mary was a Jewish woman during the time of Jesus, married to a man named Clopas. She appears in the Gospel accounts as one of the women who accompanied Jesus and His disciples (John 19:25).
2. She is identified as the mother of James the Less and Joses, two of the companions or relatives of Jesus mentioned in the Gospels (Matthew 27:56, Mark 15:40).
3. Her devotion to Jesus is manifested by her presence at the foot of the cross — she was among the women who left everything to follow the Lord until His last moment. She is also mentioned as a witness of the resurrection, going to the tomb on Easter morning (Matthew 28:1, Mark 16:1, Luke 24:10).
G3137K.origine: The name Mary comes from the Aramaic מַרְיָם (Maryam) and the Hebrew מִרְיָם (Miryam), the exact meaning of which remains debated by scholars. In the Greek New Testament, the name is written in two forms: Μαρία (Maria, Greek form) and Μαριάμ (Mariam, Aramaic form retained). It was a very common name in first-century Israel — several important women in the New Testament bear it.
G3137K.emploi: The New Testament mentions several women named Mary, and this entry specifically concerns Mary, wife of Clopas. She first appears in the account of the crucifixion (John 19:25), where she stands near the cross alongside the mother of Jesus. The other three Gospel writers also mention her during the discovery of the empty tomb: she was among the women who went to the sepulcher on the morning of the resurrection to anoint Jesus' body. Although briefly mentioned, she is presented as a courageous and faithful disciple, present at the two decisive moments — the death and resurrection — of the Lord.
G3137K.portee: Mary of Clopas embodies the silent faithfulness of the women in the New Testament in the face of trial. Her presence at the cross reminds us that following Jesus means accompanying Him to the end, even when all seems lost. She encourages us to persevere in our commitment to the Lord, not for prestige or miracles, but through patient love and loving presence in the heart of suffering.

sens: mother of Jesus
Mary of Magdala
wife of Clopas, mother of James the Less
sister of Martha and Lazarus
mother of John Mark
Christian greeted by Paul
G3137L.detail: The name Mary refers to six distinct women in the New Testament. 1. The most famous is the mother of Jesus, mentioned from her conception by the angel Gabriel and present at the manger, at the wedding at Cana, at the foot of the cross, and at Pentecost (Matthew 1:16 ff., Luke 1:27 ff.). 2. Mary of Magdala, also called Mary Magdalene, is the one who poured perfume on Jesus' feet and was the first to see Him resurrected. 3. Another Mary, wife of Clopas, witnessed the crucifixion and discovered the empty tomb: she was the mother of James the Less and Joses (Matthew 27:56, Mark 15:40). 4. The sister of Martha and Lazarus, who sat at Jesus' feet to listen, while Martha was busy serving (Luke 10:39). 5. The mother of John Mark, where the apostles gathered to pray, welcomed Peter after his release from prison (Acts 12:12). 6. A Christian in Rome, greeted by the apostle Paul as someone who had worked hard for the church (Romans 16:6).
G3137L.origine: The name Mary comes from the Hebrew Miryam (מִרְיָם), the exact etymology of which remains debated by scholars. It could mean "beloved" or "mistress of the sea." It is a common Hebrew name in the Old Testament, notably borne by Moses' sister (Exodus 15:20). The Greek uses two forms: Μαρία (Maria), the Hellenized form, and Μαριάμ (Mariam), an indeclinable form closer to the original Aramaic. The latter reminds us that many of these women were Palestinian or Aramaic-speaking Jews.
G3137L.emploi: The name Mary is borne by at least six distinct women in the New Testament. The most famous remains the mother of Jesus, who appears regularly in the four Gospels: at the Annunciation (Luke 1), at the Nativity (Luke 2:5, 16), at Cana (John 2), at Calvary (John 19:25), and at Pentecost (Acts 1:14). Mary Magdalene figures in the Passion and Resurrection narratives in all the Gospels. The wife of Clopas accompanies Jesus to the tomb (Matthew 27:56-61, Mark 15:40, 47). The sister of Martha and Lazarus is presented as an attentive disciple of Jesus (Luke 10:39, 42; John 11-12). The mother of John Mark appears as an active woman who put her home at the service of the early church (Acts 12:12). Finally, a Mary in Rome is praised by Paul for her apostolic work (Romans 16:6). This multiplicity of Marys shows the importance of women in the evangelical story.
G3137L.portee: These different Marys remind us that women played essential roles in the life of Jesus and in the birth of the Church: mother, disciple, witness of the Resurrection, servant. Each, in her own way, illustrates a form of faith and commitment. Recognizing these women is to see that the Gospel liberates and values women in a culture where their role was often limited.

sens: Mother of Jesus
Woman named Mary Magdalene
Wife of Clopas and mother of James the Less
Sister of Martha and Lazarus
Mother of John Mark
Christian woman in Rome
G3137M.detail:
1. Mary, the mother of Jesus, is present from the moment of the Annunciation and throughout His earthly life: she carries Him, gives birth to Him, witnesses His ministry, and stands at the foot of His cross. She embodies trust in God despite the incomprehension of events.
2. Mary Magdalene is a woman whom Jesus healed and who becomes one of His closest disciples; she is the first to see Him resurrected.
3. This Mary, the wife of Clopas, stood near the cross and was among the first to discover the empty tomb. She is the mother of James the Less and Joses.
4. Mary of Bethany, sister of Martha, sits at Jesus' feet to listen to Him and anoints His feet with perfume as a sign of devotion and love.
5. This Mary is the mother of John Mark, whose house in Jerusalem becomes a meeting place for the disciples after Pentecost.
6. Mary of Rome is a Christian woman whom Paul greets for her zealous work in the service of the Church and the Lord.
G3137M.origine: The name Mary is the Hellenized Greek form (Maria) of an Aramaic and Hebrew root (Myriam). The exact meaning of the Hebrew name is not definitively established, but it is often associated with a root meaning "bitterness" or "beloved." It was a common name in the first-century Jewish community, borne by several important women in the life of Jesus and the early Church.
G3137M.emploi: The name Mary refers to six different women in the New Testament, each playing a distinct role in the Gospel and apostolic narrative. The most famous is Mary of Nazareth, the mother of Jesus, mentioned at the beginning of the Gospel of Matthew and present at key moments in Christ's life. Other Marys appear as disciples, as witnesses of the Passion and Resurrection, or as women engaged in the service of the Church. In Romans 16:6, Paul greets a Mary for her labor in the Lord, showing that the name was common and that several women bore this name in the early churches.
G3137M.portee: These different Marys embody various forms of devotion and faith: the mother who accepts the mystery of God's plan, the disciples who follow Jesus despite dangers, the women who serve generously. Their examples show that faith is not reserved for men and that women play an essential role in the history of salvation and in the life of the Church.

sens: Collaborator of Paul and Barnabas in the apostolic ministry
Author of the Gospel according to Mark
Cousin of Barnabas
G3138.detail:
1. Mark is a young Christian man from Jerusalem, the son of Mary, a woman who welcomes the apostles in prayer in her house (Acts 12:12). He joins Barnabas and Paul for their missionary work but leaves them partway through in Pamphylia, which causes a disagreement between his two companions (Acts 15:37-39).

2. Mark later becomes a valuable collaborator of Paul, to the point that the apostle specifically requests him from Timothy to assist in his ministry (2 Timothy 4:11). Peter also mentions him as being with him (1 Peter 5:13), indicating that he circulates among the different leaders of the Church.

3. Mark is the cousin of Barnabas (Colossians 4:10), which explains the close bond between these two men and their departure together for Cyprus after their separation from Paul.
G3138.origine: The Greek name Μάρκος (Markos) is the Greek form of the Latin name Marcus. It is a common Roman cognomen, but John, the character's true Semitic name (Acts 12:12, 25), indicates that he is a Jew who also bears this Latin name — a common practice among Jews of the diaspora in the first century.
G3138.emploi: Mark appears in eight passages of the New Testament, all in Acts and the epistles. He is first presented as a young man from Jerusalem associated with Paul and Barnabas in their first missionary journey (Acts 12:25), which he abandons midway (Acts 15:37-39). Paul refuses to take him back due to this failure, leading to a conflict with Barnabas. However, Mark redeems himself: he becomes valuable to Paul (2 Timothy 4:11), works with the other apostles, particularly Peter (1 Peter 5:13), and Paul holds him in such high regard that he recommends his reception to the Colossians (Colossians 4:10). These passages illustrate the redemption of a man who initially faltered but proved trustworthy.
G3138.portee: Mark's story teaches the believer that initial failure is not final. Rejected once by Paul for his lack of perseverance, he demonstrates that grace transforms the weak man into a faithful worker. For the Christian who has faced setbacks, Mark's example offers hope that repentance and perseverance restore trust and enable true service.

sens: white or colored crystalline stone, hard and shiny, polished for construction and decoration
in a context of wealth and luxury
G3139.detail:
1. Marble is a hard, crystalline natural stone, shiny when polished, highly valued for its beautiful veins and varied colors. Its Greek name comes from a verb meaning "to shine," which reflects how the ancients viewed this stone: luminous and sparkling. It has been used since antiquity to construct prestigious buildings, temples, and palaces, and to sculpt statues.
2. In Revelation, marble appears in the list of riches that the commercial world boasts: "cargo of gold, silver, precious stones... in marble" (Revelation 18:12). Here, the word denotes not only the material but also the symbol of earthly luxury and opulence — the precious goods in which humans place their trust rather than in God.
G3139.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb "marmairô" which means "to shine" or "to sparkle." This origin well expresses the nature of the stone: crystalline, polished, reflective. Marble was already known and appreciated in ancient Greece for the construction of temples and sculpture. The French word "marbre" is derived directly from this.
G3139.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 18:12. John lists the goods that the merchants of the world lament not being able to sell at the fall of Babylon. Marble is mentioned alongside gold, silver, pearls, and fine fabrics: these are the material treasures that embody the power and luxury of human civilization separated from God. The context shows that John is not speaking of marble as a mere building material, but as a luxury good, a reflection of covetousness and pride.
G3139.portee: The mention of marble in this apocalyptic context invites the reader to consider all that shines and attracts desire on earth — even what seems durable and precious — as transient and destined to disappear. It calls for a detachment from material wealth and vigilance against the seduction of luxury, directing one's trust instead toward Christ and the eternal Kingdom.

sens: to affirm what one has personally seen or heard
to solemnly declare the truth about something or someone
to give a favorable report about someone, to approve
to serve as evidence or confirmation
G3140.detail:
1. To testify means to affirm what one has personally seen or heard, like a witness in court. John testifies to what he has seen and heard (John 3:32), and Jesus declares: "I testify about myself" (John 8:18). It is to speak from firsthand knowledge, as a direct witness.

2. It also means to solemnly declare the truth about someone or something, to convince others. The prophets testify about Christ that whoever believes in him receives the forgiveness of sins (Acts 10:43). To testify here means to publicly affirm an important truth.

3. In a softer sense, to testify can mean to approve someone, to confirm that they are worthy of esteem. Enoch received the testimony that he was pleasing to God (Hebrews 11:5): this is divine confirmation that his life was pleasing to God.

4. Finally, a testimony serves as evidence or support: the Law and the Prophets testify to the righteousness of God (Romans 3:21), providing proof of it.
G3140.origine: The word comes from "martus" (martyr, witness), one who sees and reports what he has seen. In ancient Hebrew, the word "ед" (witness) is the root of the verb that primarily means "to be present" or "to see." The French verb "rendre témoignage" retains this image of ocular presence and faithful reporting of what one has seen.
G3140.emploi: This verb is used 73 times in the New Testament, especially in the Gospel of John (about 30 times) and in the Epistles. John uses it to speak of the testimony that John the Baptist gives about Jesus (John 1:7-8, 15), the testimony of Jesus about himself (John 8:18), and the testimony of the Spirit (John 15:26-27). In Acts, it refers to the apostles' testimony about the resurrection (Acts 10:43) and the approval received from other believers (Acts 6:3, 10:22). In Paul, it can express a solemn deposition against someone (1 Corinthians 15:15) or a good report (Galatians 4:15). The basic meaning is always to faithfully report what one knows or has seen.
G3140.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that faith rests on received testimony. The apostles are witnesses of the resurrection (Acts 10:43: all the prophets testify about Christ). To testify oneself is also an act of faith: speaking of what God has done in one's life is participating in the apostolic testimony. That is why Jesus tells his disciples: "you have said that you will testify about the one who sent you" (John 15:27) — it is a responsibility and a privilege.

sens: What a person reports after having seen or heard something
Solemn declaration before a court or judges
Evidence, element that establishes the truth of a statement
Message or announcement of good news, especially that of Jesus Christ
G3141.detail:
1. Testimony is primarily what someone reports after being a witness. It is the direct account of a person who has seen or heard the facts themselves. John says about this: "who bore witness to the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ, all that he saw" (Revelation 1:2). It is an authentic account based on personal experience.
2. Testimony takes an official and solemn form in court. During Jesus' trial, the religious leaders "sought testimony against Jesus, to put him to death" (Mark 14:55): they were looking for a statement that could condemn him. The law stipulated: "the testimony of two men is true" (John 8:17), meaning that at least two witnesses are needed to establish the truth of a serious claim.
3. Testimony becomes evidence, a piece of evidence that establishes the truth. Jesus declares: "the testimony that he bears about me is true" (John 5:32). A testimony can be true or false, credible or not: that is why John warns: "You receive the testimony of men; the testimony of God is greater" (1 John 5:9).
4. In the New Testament, the term particularly refers to the message about Jesus Christ and his works. The disciples testify to his resurrection (Acts 22:18), and at the end of times, some are killed "because of the testimony of Jesus" (Revelation 12:17). It is a key term in Christian preaching.
G3141.origine: The Greek word "marturia" comes from the verb "martureô" (to testify), which itself comes from "martus" (witness). Originally, a witness is someone who has witnessed an event and can speak about it. In Hebrew, the word "edut" (testimony, attested law) and "ed" (witness) are the equivalents that the Greek translation of the Old Testament uses to convey this same meaning. Testimony is therefore fundamentally linked to lived experience and the reliable communication of truth.
G3141.emploi: The word appears 36 times in the New Testament, especially in John and Revelation. In the Gospels, it primarily refers to testimony in a judicial sense: during Jesus' trial, the religious authorities seek one to condemn him, but the testimonies collected prove contradictory (Mark 14:55-59). John uses it 13 times to speak of testimony in favor of Jesus: John the Baptist bears witness (John 1:19), Jesus asserts that the Father's testimony about him surpasses all human testimony (John 5:31-36), and the evangelist himself guarantees the authenticity of his account (John 19:35, 21:24). In Revelation, the term takes on a tone of proclamation and commitment: those who keep "the testimony of Jesus" are worthy of reward (Revelation 12:17, 19:10), and it is even a cause of martyrdom (Revelation 12:11). In Paul and Titus, testimony is linked to reputation and good moral conduct (1 Timothy 3:7, Titus 1:13).
G3141.portee: For the Christian reading the Bible, testimony raises a decisive question: on what foundation does he place his trust in Jesus? The Gospels do not offer legal proof, but testimonies from those who have seen and believed. Believing in the biblical testimony means trusting the integrity and authenticity of these witnesses. Furthermore, the word reminds us that every Christian is called to be a witness: not by invoking a legal rule, but by sharing what he has seen and heard from God in his own life. It is a call to faithfulness and honesty.

sens: Declaration that confirms or proves something
Concrete evidence of a fact or a healing
Report that accounts for something
Personal attestation of what one has seen or heard
Visible and speaking presence of someone before others
The Holy Place, tent where God manifests Himself
G3142.detail:
1. A testimony is a solemn declaration intended to prove something. In Matthew 8:4, Jesus orders the leper to show himself to the priest so that his healing may be a testimony — the proof that the miracle has taken place.
2. Sometimes, the word refers to the proof itself: the concrete act that shows the reality of something. In Acts 4:33, the apostles were giving testimony to the resurrection of the Lord through their words and actions.
3. The testimony can also be the declaration made to an authority or a judge. When Jesus tells the disciples that they will be brought before governors, it will be a testimony for them (Matthew 10:18) — the opportunity to declare their faith publicly.
4. In Paul’s writings, testimony also becomes the personal attestation of what one has lived and experienced: in 2 Corinthians 1:12, it is the testimony of his conscience, the report of his own life to God.
5. Sometimes the word takes on a broader meaning: the visible presence and action by which someone affirms who they are. In 2 Timothy 1:8, giving testimony to the Lord means showing and defending Him through one’s life and words.
6. In the Old Testament, the tent of testimony (Acts 7:44) is the place where God dwells among His people, which testifies to His presence.
G3142.origine: The word comes from the Greek root μάρτυ- (martyr-, witness), the same root that produces martyr. In Acts 7:44, it translates the Hebrew expression אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד ("tent of meeting"), the tabernacle where God meets with Israel. The word carries the idea of something or someone who rises up to show the truth: a witness who speaks, a proof that cries out.
G3142.emploi: The word appears 19 times in the New Testament, especially in the Synoptics (Matthew, Mark, Luke) and the letters of Paul. In the Synoptics, it often refers to the declaration made before authorities (Matthew 10:18, 24:14; Mark 13:9; Luke 21:13) — it is a public act by which one confesses their faith. In Acts, it takes on a more active tone: the apostles were giving testimony, meaning they were publicly proclaiming and proving the resurrection (4:33). In Paul’s writings, the word becomes more introspective: it is the testimony of his conscience (2 Corinthians 1:12) or the call to testify about the Lord (2 Timothy 1:8). In Revelation and Hebrews, it returns to the concrete meaning: the tent of testimony, the sanctuary where God manifests Himself (Acts 7:44; Revelation 15:5).
G3142.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that faith is never secret or silent: it shows and declares itself. Giving testimony is publicly affirming what God has done and what one has experienced of Him — through words and through life. It is also being aware that our simple existence, if it reflects God’s grace, can be a living testimony for others. The word calls for faithfulness: may our testimony be a true proclamation of who the Lord is.

sens: Call someone to testify, cite them as a witness
Affirm or protest with force and gravity
Beseech or urge someone to do something
G3143.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to call someone to testify before a judge or an assembly, as one would summon a witness to the stand. This is the underlying image: invoking someone’s testimony.
2. From this comes the meaning of affirming or protesting solemnly, engaging one’s own word. When Paul says in Acts 20:26, "I declare to you that I am innocent of the blood of all of you," he forcefully asserts that he is not responsible for the fate of his listeners, putting his conscience on the line.
3. The word can also mean to beseech or urge someone insistently: in Ephesians 4:17, Paul "declares" to the Ephesians not to walk as the Gentiles do, which is almost a solemn order, a pressing call to obey.
G3143.origine: The word comes from the root *martyr* (witness) and the middle verb (*-omai*), which expresses an action that the subject performs for their own interest or by committing themselves. It literally means "to present oneself as a witness" or "to testify for oneself." The word family includes *martys* (witness), *martyria* (testimony), and *martureo* (to testify). The Greek verb often translates the Hebrew *'ud* when speaking of testifying or attesting to something.
G3143.emploi: The verb appears only 4 times in the New Testament, always in contexts where the apostle Paul or someone in authority affirms or protests something with insistence. In Acts 20:26, Paul declares himself innocent of the blood of those who have not listened to him; in Galatians 5:3, he solemnly protests against the imposed circumcision. In Acts 26:22, he bears witness to what he has seen and heard; in Ephesians 4:17, he urges the Ephesians to change their lives. The word always marks a statement imbued with authority or urgency, an affirmation that the speaker wants to weigh with all their weight.
G3143.portee: This word shows how the apostle Paul seals his teachings with particular gravity: he does not merely propose, he declares, he protests, he beseeches. It is a lesson for the Christian: certain truths of the Gospel must be proclaimed not as opinions, but as solemn affirmations, charged with urgency and authority. This reminds us that faith is not an indifferent matter: it engages the one who testifies and calls the one who listens to respond.

sens: A person who has seen or heard something and can attest to it
One who testifies before a court or assembly
One who attests to the truth of faith in Christ by their life or death
A person called to guarantee the truth of a word or commitment
That which serves as proof or testimony of something
G3144.detail:
1. A witness is primarily someone who has been present, who has seen with their eyes or heard with their ears. Peter tells the disciples: "You will be my witness in Jerusalem" (Acts 1:22), meaning one who recounts what they have personally known of the risen Christ. This is the very foundation of testimony: direct experience.

2. In a legal or official context, a witness is called to testify: Jesus says that a matter will be settled "on the testimony of two or three witnesses" (Matthew 18:16). False witnesses (Acts 6:13) are those who lie to accuse someone. This is a serious and regulated role.

3. For the early Christians, a witness can be someone who suffers or dies for their faith in Christ — which the Greek word itself will eventually designate specifically. Stephen and others who shed their blood for Christ are witnesses in the deepest sense (Revelation 2:13, 17:6).

4. A witness can also be called simply to guarantee an act or word, as when Paul invokes God as a witness: "I call God as my witness" (Romans 1:9), meaning: God knows that I speak the truth.

5. Finally, a person or thing can serve as a witness in the sense of living proof. Hebrews 12:1 speaks of a "cloud of witnesses," meaning those whose previous example attests that faith in God is possible and victorious.
G3144.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "to see," hence the image of the witness as one who has seen. The Greek form μάρτυς regularly translates the Hebrew word עֵד ("ed") in the Greek Old Testament, which has exactly the same meaning: one who sees and reports. The family of the Greek word includes the verb μαρτυρέω (to testify, to bear witness), which shows that being a witness is primarily an act: to attest to what one has seen.
G3144.emploi: The word is used 35 times in the New Testament, especially in Acts and Revelation. It primarily refers to witnesses in the ordinary sense: those who can attest to a fact before judges or an assembly (Matthew 18:16, 26:65, Acts 6:13). But the usage gradually becomes broader and more theological. In Acts, the apostles are witnesses of the resurrection of Christ: they have seen the Risen One and report it (Acts 1:22, 2:32, 5:32, 10:39, 26:16). Paul in Acts 22:15 is called to be a "witness" to all men. Then the word takes on a martial and spiritual dimension: one who testifies for Christ risks their life, and Christian martyrdom arises from this reality (Acts 22:20, Revelation 2:13). Christ himself is called "the faithful witness" (Revelation 1:5, 3:14), for he attests to the truth of God through his life and death.
G3144.portee: For the Christian reader, this word raises questions about what they have received from God and how they convey it. Being a witness is not a burden reserved for the apostles alone: every Christian is called to testify to what they have experienced of the grace and truth of Christ. The word also reminds us of the importance of consistency between word and life: a true witness engages their credibility, and in ultimate cases, their life. Finally, it shows us that a powerful faith relies on lived testimonies, not on abstractions.

sens: To bite with the teeth, to chew
G3145.detail: 1. To bite with the teeth, to chew: this is the physical action of seizing and tearing with the teeth. In Revelation 16:10, during the fifth plague, men bite their tongues in extreme pain — this gesture expresses their intolerable suffering in the face of the darkness that covers the kingdom of the beast.
G3145.origine: The word comes from a root expressing the action of chewing or biting. It is rare in classical Greek (good ancient authors avoid it), but appears in later writers and in popular literature. The Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament) uses it in Job 30:4 to describe people who eat roots — the word thus also denotes the action of chewing.
G3145.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in Revelation 16:10. It describes a gesture of extreme pain: men, tortured by the miraculous darkness that strikes the kingdom of the beast, bite their tongues. This graphic detail underscores the intensity of the suffering inflicted by divine judgment. The context of Revelation makes it a sign of despair and hopeless distress.
G3145.portee: This verse reminds us that God's judgment is fearsome and produces real and incomprehensible suffering for those who rebel against him. The gesture of biting one's tongue evokes the frustration and powerless rage of those who refuse to repent even in the face of obvious signs of judgment. For the Christian reader, it serves as a solemn warning.

sens: To strike someone with a rod or whip
To inflict corporal punishment, particularly a legal sentence
To exercise correction or discipline from one who has authority
G3146.detail:
1. The word designates the action of striking violently with a flexible instrument like a rod or whip. It is a direct physical punishment: Pilate "had Jesus beaten with rods" (John 19:1) before his crucifixion, a well-known Roman torture.
2. It also evokes an officially imposed judicial punishment. The Jewish authorities threatened to "beat with rods" the disciples in the synagogues (Matthew 10:17), as a legal punishment authorized by their laws.
3. In a figurative sense, it expresses a father's correction of his son: God "disciplines every son he receives" (Hebrews 12:6), meaning he corrects him as a father corrects his child for his good, not out of cruelty.
G3146.origine: The word comes from μάστιξ (mastix), which literally means "rod" or "whip." It is a very ancient instrument of punishment in the Mediterranean world, used by both Romans and Jewish authorities. The root evokes the idea of striking, of correcting through physical violence. In the Septuagint (the Greek version of the Old Testament), this verb often translates the Hebrew "to strike" or "to correct."
G3146.emploi: The verb appears 6 times in the Gospels, always to describe the torture inflicted on Jesus or the threat of punishment against his disciples. Matthew, Mark, and Luke recount that Jesus was beaten with rods by the Romans (Matthew 20:19, Mark 10:34, Luke 18:33, John 19:1), and that the synagogues threatened the apostles with similar treatment (Matthew 10:17, Matthew 23:34). Only one figurative occurrence appears in Hebrews 12:6, where the verb speaks of divine correction: God "disciplines" those he loves, an image borrowed from Proverbs 3:12, to express not a destructive violence but a formative discipline.
G3146.portee: This word reminds us of the real violence that Jesus suffered for us, a concrete physical suffering that precedes his crucifixion. For the reader, it helps to measure the price of redemption, not as a theological abstraction but as a painful bodily act. The figurative use in Hebrews also invites us to see God's hand in the trials of life: a correction that comes from love, not from hatred.

sens: To strike someone with a whip or rod
To inflict physical correction with a whip
G3147.detail:
1. The word refers to the action of striking someone with a whip or rod, which is an instrument made of cords or strips. It is a practice of corporal punishment in the ancient world. In Acts 22:25, Paul opposes being whipped without judgment: "Is it lawful for you to scourge a Roman citizen?"
2. In a figurative or extended sense, the word can refer to any severe correction inflicted by whipping, such as legal punishment or chastisement. The image is one of physical pain inflicted by repeated blows.
G3147.origine: The Greek word mastizō comes from mastix, which means "whip" or "rod." This family of words describes the instrument of punishment and its action. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, similar verbs (like naka in the hiphil) express striking or beating. The word belongs to the classical and biblical Greek vocabulary of corporal punishment.
G3147.emploi: The verb mastizō appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 22:25, in the episode where Paul defends his rights as a Roman citizen. He invokes Roman law to refuse to be whipped without trial. This unique usage shows how the practice of whipping was common in Roman administration but subject to legal rules. The context highlights the difference between Roman justice and Jewish judicial practices.
G3147.portee: This word reminds Christians that Paul himself experienced violence and mistreatment, but he also knew how to defend the dignity granted to him by law. It invites the reader to reflect on justice and the limits of correction, as well as the courage of one who dares to oppose power to affirm the truth.

sens: instrument of correction made of strips
instrument of torture or punishment
sickness or suffering sent by God as punishment
G3148.detail:
1. The whip is a physical instrument made of strips, used to strike and punish. In Acts 22:24, the Romans want to "examine by scourging" Paul to make him speak — it is a means of brutal interrogation.

2. Metaphorically, the Bible also calls any suffering or sickness that God sends as correction a "whip." Mark 3:10 reports that people who came to Jesus had "diseases" (the same Greek word); Mark 5:29 and 5:34 speak of the "affliction" from which a woman suffered. These diseases are not blows, but the Bible designates them with this word for whip because they come from God and discipline the one who endures them, just as a whip would discipline the body.
G3148.origine: The word μάστιξ comes from a Greek root that evokes the idea of striking. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew שׁוֹט (shot) which literally means a whip or strap. This image of the whip as an instrument of God — who strikes to correct and bring back to Him — is a central theme of biblical wisdom: the suffering sent by God is compared to a parental whip.
G3148.emploi: This word appears 6 times in the New Testament. Three times it refers to the physical whip: in Acts 22:24, where the Romans prepare a whip to torture Paul; in Hebrews 11:36, where martyrs endured the whip alongside chains and imprisonment. Three times it metaphorically refers to sickness: Mark 3:10, Mark 5:29, and 5:34 speak of "affliction" or "disease" as a whip, and Luke 7:21 uses the same word for the "infirmities" that Jesus heals. This shift from a concrete meaning to a figurative one shows how the Bible viewed sickness: not merely as a medical event, but as an action of God that disciplines.
G3148.portee: This word reminds us that, for the Bible, sickness and suffering are never neutral: they come from God and aim to correct and transform the one who endures them. But the heart of the Gospel is that Jesus heals from these "whips" — He absorbs the correction we deserved. Understanding this word helps the believer see their suffering not as a blind punishment, but as an opportunity for an encounter with the God who heals and forgives.

sens: Woman's breast, particularly considered as a source of nourishment for the child
Chest, front part of the thorax
G3149.detail:
1. The breast is the woman's breast, particularly viewed in its nourishing role: it is the organ that breastfeeds. In Luke 11:27, a woman cries out to Jesus: "Blessed is the breast that nursed you!", thinking of the one who bore and nourished Jesus as a child. Similarly, in Luke 23:29, Jesus speaks of women blessed not to have breastfed — He then evokes the sufferings that physical motherhood will bring in times of distress. The word concentrates the image of life given, of the nurturing maternal bond.
2. By extension, the word can refer to the chest in general, the front part of the thorax — not just the lactation organ, but the region of the heart and breath. It is in this sense that Revelation 1:13 speaks of the Son of Man "having a golden sash around the chest," a detail of clothing and majesty.
G3149.origine: The Greek word μαστός comes from an ancient root that designates breastfeeding and nursing. In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses the word שַׁד ("shad") to refer to the breast, particularly in passages concerning breastfeeding and fertility (Genesis 49:25 speaks of blessings "from the breasts and the womb"). Greek takes up this fundamental image: the breast as a source of life and nourishment.
G3149.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, only in Luke and Revelation, and always in the plural. In Luke, it expresses the honor given to the physical motherhood of Mary in Luke 11:27, then the misfortune of mothers during future calamities in Luke 23:29 — Jesus speaks not of the joy of breastfeeding, but of the grief of a mother who loses her child. In Revelation, the term moves away from breastfeeding to simply designate the chest of the Son of Man in His vision of heavenly glory. The context thus determines whether the word evokes nurturing motherhood or merely the region of the body.
G3149.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus had a mother, Mary, who bore and breastfed Him: it affirms His true incarnation, His complete humanity. In Luke 23:29, Jesus does not despise motherhood, but warns that the sufferings to come will make maternal bonds terrible — it is a word of compassion about the human cost of destruction. For the believer, this word maintains the humanity of Christ and the reality of His mother in history.

sens: hollow and unfounded words
futile chatter that diverts from the truth
talk that misleads and causes one to lose track of Christian teaching
G3150.detail:
1. Empty talk refers to words that sound hollow, devoid of real meaning or lasting value. It is weightless chatter, comparable to wind: much is said, but nothing important is conveyed. In 1 Timothy 1:6, Paul speaks of some who "have strayed into empty talk" — empty words that contribute nothing to faith.
2. By extension, it is chatter that diverts from what truly matters. These futile words lead away from essential truths, solid faith, and sincere love. They cause one to forget or lose sight of the essence of the Christian message.
3. For Paul, empty talk characterizes one who has missed their spiritual target: instead of seeking true love and a good conscience, one strays into sterile debates and hollow words that serve no purpose.
G3150.origine: The Greek word comes from two roots: "empty" (mataia-, meaning hollow, worthless) and "talk, word" (logia-, from the verb to speak). It is exactly like saying in French "empty-word." The word paints the image of someone who talks a lot but says nothing — pure wind. This notion of empty or hollow speech is also found in the Greek Old Testament when referring to futile or unfounded things.
G3150.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 1:6. Paul uses it to warn Timothy: some Christians have "turned away" from the essentials and have "strayed into empty talk." The context suggests that it likely refers to sterile theological debates or false teachings that contribute nothing to true faith. Paul contrasts this empty talk with what should be central for a Christian: sincere love, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith. The term emphasizes the contrast between hollow words and truly constructive speech in the life of faith.
G3150.portee: This word warns us of the danger of hollow speech and empty chatter in the Christian life. It invites us to examine our discourse, our debates, our words: do they serve to build up faith, deepen love for God and neighbor, or are they just wind? It is a call to vigilance: not to be diverted by futile talk, but to return to what truly matters — sincere love and truth.

sens: A person who talks a lot without saying anything solid
One who produces hollow and useless words
A chatterer who charms with empty speeches
G3151.detail:
1. An empty talker is someone who speaks a lot, but their words are devoid of real content and value. It is the chatterer who fills the air with words without bringing anything substantial — imagine someone who discourses, listens to themselves talk, but whose remarks lead nowhere.
2. This hollow speech is often alluring or flattering: the empty talker seeks to impress or convince, but without a solid foundation. In Titus 1:10, the Apostle Paul denounces these "empty talkers" among the circumcised who seduce the faithful with words that sound good but lead away from Christian truth.
3. Thus, they are deceptive speakers: not honestly silent or discreet, but someone whose very speech is the problem — it deceives because it is vain, hollow, lacking weight and truth.
G3151.origine: The Greek word combines "mataios" (vain, useless, without substance) and "logos" (word, speech). It literally means "one whose speech is vain." The initial image is that of emptiness: a word that has no weight, fruit, or reality behind it. The word opposes any speech that is full, serious, true, and beneficial.
G3151.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Titus 1:10. Paul uses it to designate adversaries — rebellious people, circumcised, who disturb the communities with their seductive but deceitful speeches. The Apostle groups them with seducers, which shows that empty speech is an instrument of seduction and diversion from faith. This context reveals that the empty talker is not a mere harmless chatterer, but a spiritual danger.
G3151.portee: This word invites us to discern: the richness of a word does not lie in its volume, eloquence, or charm, but in its truth and spiritual fruit. For the listening Christian, it is a call to test words by the Word of God. For the speaker, it is a warning: to avoid the vanity of speech, seeking to build up through truth rather than merely the brilliance of words.

sens: That produces no result, that is ineffective or useless
That is hollow, devoid of meaning or substance
That is false or deceptive
That pertains to idols or gods without reality
Referring to a word or thought that leads nowhere
G3152.detail:
1. The word primarily describes what is unproductive, ineffective: a vain faith does not save (1 Corinthians 15:17), a vain religion that does not transform the heart is worthless (James 1:26), vain discussions serve no purpose (Titus 3:9). It is the image of an effort that leads to nothing, of a seed that does not sprout.

2. The word also applies to what is hollow, empty of truth: the vain thoughts of the wise, which God sees as devoid of real wisdom (1 Corinthians 3:20).

3. It qualifies what is deceptive or inherited from lies: a vain way of life, passed down from the fathers (1 Peter 1:18), meaning based on illusions.

4. Finally, the word designates idols and false gods: the men in Acts 14:15 worshiped vain things, meaning gods that are nothing but emptiness.
G3152.origine: The word μάταιος comes from a root meaning "in vain, empty." In Hebrew, it often translates שָׁוְא ("lie, deception") and הֶבֶל ("vanity, that which evaporates"), particularly in Ecclesiastes. The initial image is that of emptiness, of what dissipates or fills nothing. The adverb μάτην ("in vain") belongs to the same family.
G3152.emploi: The word appears six times in the New Testament, always in a critical perspective. In 1 Corinthians 15:17, it refers to faith without resurrection: it loses its strength. In 1 Corinthians 3:20 and Titus 3:9, it refers to human thoughts and words detached from God. In James 1:26 and 1 Peter 1:18, μάταιος qualifies religious or moral life that has only appearance without substance. In Acts 14:15, the apostles call the pagans to flee the worship of idols, which they name vain things. The word always emphasizes the absence of real effect or true substance.
G3152.portee: This word invites the reader to discern the difference between appearance and spiritual reality. A nominal faith, a façade piety, human wisdom without God, or any form of idolatry are vain: they produce neither salvation nor transformation. Μάταιος calls the Christian to seek what has weight and truth: the risen Christ, the Word of God, a heart obedience.

sens: The empty and insubstantial nature of something
The state of a project or desire that leads to nothing
The futility of a thought or occupation without foundation
The pride that leads to self-sufficiency and appearance
G3153.detail:
1. Vanity refers to what is hollow, without substance or lasting value. It is the absence of meaning or solidity — like a bubble that bursts. Romans 8:20 speaks of creation subjected to this vanity: even material things do not offer definitive satisfaction; they degrade and disappear.

2. It also signifies uselessness, that which produces no result. A vain effort, an empty promise — anything that does not keep its promises. In Ephesians 4:17, Paul refers to the thoughts of the Gentiles: they seem full of wisdom, but they are barren, without true connection to God, thus without lasting fruit.

3. The word also evokes lightness, the inconsistency of a word or thought that is not based on anything solid. In 2 Peter 2:18, false teachers speak with "puffed-up vanity"; their words, inflated with pride, have no substance, they are just wind meant to deceive.

4. By extension, vanity can denote pride — the attachment to one's image and appearance rather than to reality. This is why this word encompasses both the objective uselessness of something and the folly of one who clings to it.
G3153.origine: The word comes from the Greek "mataia," which means "vain, futile." It is formed from a root evoking something light, weightless, that flies away. In the Greek Old Testament, it regularly translates the Hebrew "hebel" (Ecclesiastes uses it about forty times), which literally means "bubble" or "breath" — the perfect image of what is ephemeral and empty. Forms of this word are also found in Greek secular texts to express absurdity or uselessness.
G3153.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament. Paul uses it in Romans 8:20 to describe the state of the entire creation, degraded by sin: it is subjected to vanity, that is, destined for wear and death. In Ephesians 4:17, he qualifies the thoughts of the Gentiles: they are vain because they do not acknowledge God and remain empty of truth. Finally, Peter stigmatizes in 2 Peter 2:18 the false prophets whose discourse, inflated with vanity, is pure seductive spectacle. The word reveals each time the insufficiency of what opposes divine wisdom: creation without God, human thought without revelation, words without spiritual foundation.
G3153.portee: Vanity reminds the Christian that everything not anchored in God is fragile, inconsistent, and ultimately disappointing — money, glory, pleasures, proud thoughts. This word calls us not to be seduced by appearance or by empty promises. It invites us to build our lives on the unshakeable rock of God's word, not on sand. Recognizing the vanity of the world means seeking in Christ the true substance and life.

sens: To render vain, without foundation, ineffective
To plunge into mental confusion, to lose common sense
G3154.detail:
1. The verb means to make something vain or ineffective: it is to remove from a thought, project, or heart its solidity and value. In Romans 1:21, Paul says that those who knew God "became futile in their thoughts": that is, their reflections, once capable of leading to the knowledge of God, have become hollow and unfounded, like rotting wood that collapses.
2. The word also describes the mental state of someone who loses grip on reality: a heart "without understanding" (Romans 1:21) is a heart rendered inoperative, plunged into darkness, unable to see the truth. This is the result of refusing God's clarity: thoughts wrap around themselves and become barren.
G3154.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective "mataios" (vain, futile, without substance); it derives from it in the verbal form. The root evokes the idea of something hollow or empty. In biblical Greek, this word often translates the Hebrew "habal" (vanity), which appears notably in Ecclesiastes to express the futile nature of what is done without God. The basic image is that of wind, of breath: something that seems important but leaves no trace.
G3154.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 1:21. Paul uses it in his diagnosis of pagan religions: those who knew God through His visible work (Romans 1:19-20) have willfully turned away and allowed their thoughts to become vain. They did not glorify God nor give thanks to Him; instead, they became led astray. This is a pivotal moment in the text: the verb marks the shift from knowledge to error, from clarity to darkness, not by ignorance but by refusal and diversion.
G3154.portee: This word invites the Christian to measure the cost of ingratitude and intellectual pride. To be led astray in one's thoughts is to refuse to relate to the Creator what one understands of His work; it risks making the heart barren. Conversely, gratitude towards God (Romans 1:21) keeps thoughts clear and the heart rooted in truth.

sens: Without result, without effect
Without foundation, without justification
Uselessly, without valid reason
G3155.detail:
1. In vain means that the action undertaken does not lead to anything, that it remains without effect or result. Worship rendered in vain is worship that bears no fruit, that does not have the value attributed to it. In Matthew 15:9, people honor God in vain because their worship is based on human commandments instead of the true word of God.
2. It also expresses the absence of foundation or justification: an action that has no real reason for being. Teachings that contradict God's law are vain because they do not originate from divine will.
3. More broadly, in vain denotes uselessness, effort that serves no purpose. This is why Mark 7:7 repeats exactly the same word: honoring God without obeying His word is to expend one's energy and piety for nothing.
G3155.origine: The Greek word matēn comes from a root that evokes fault, wandering, or folly (matē). It appears in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) to translate Hebrew terms that express vanity and uselessness, such as hebel (vanity) and shav (the false, the empty). It is therefore a rich word that carries the idea of failure not only practically but also morally and spiritually.
G3155.emploi: The word matēn is used only twice in the Gospels of Matthew and Mark, both in quotations from the prophet Isaiah (Isaiah 29:13 in the Septuagint). Jesus uses it to criticize the hypocritical worship of the religious leaders of His time: they honor God outwardly with their lips and observances, but their hearts are far from Him, and their teachings are human inventions, not divine commandments. In both passages, the context is that of the conflict between true piety (that which comes from God) and false piety (that which comes from men). The word thus expresses the spiritual and moral ineffectiveness of a religious practice detached from the real will of God.
G3155.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds a crucial truth: a religious life without sincere obedience from the heart, a facade of piety, or zeal based on human traditions rather than on the word of God, all of this remains vain. It is a call to authenticity: honoring God in vain means deceiving oneself. True worship, true honor given to God, must spring from a genuinely converted heart and obey divine revelation, not human precepts.

sens: Apostle of Jesus, former tax collector
Disciple who followed Jesus and participated in His mission
Presumed author of the Gospel according to Matthew
G3156.detail: 1. Matthew is a man whom Jesus called while he was working as a tax collector (publican) sitting at the tax booth. At this call, he immediately left his job and followed Jesus (Matthew 9:9). 2. After his calling, Matthew became one of the twelve apostles of Jesus, alongside Peter, John, James, and the other disciples. His name appears in all four lists of the apostles: in Matthew where he is explicitly called "the tax collector," in Mark, Luke, and in Acts (Matthew 10:3, Mark 3:18, Luke 6:15, Acts 1:13). 3. Christian tradition considers Matthew to be the author of the Gospel that bears his name, although this is not explicitly stated in the provided biblical text.
G3156.origine: The name Matthew comes from the Hebrew Mattityahu (Matthaios in Greek), which means "gift of the Lord" or "gift of God." It is formed from two Hebrew roots: "mattan" (gift) and "Yah" (abbreviation of the name of God). This name reflects the belief that this disciple, called to follow Jesus while he was a tax collector, represented a special grace from the Lord. In the Gospels, he is also called Levi, his other name.
G3156.emploi: Matthew appears five times in the New Testament, always identified as one of the twelve apostles. His calling as a tax collector is the moment of his conversion (Matthew 9:9), making him a remarkable example of transformation by Jesus. He is named in the four apostolic lists of the synoptics and Acts (Matthew 10:3, Mark 3:18, Luke 6:15, Acts 1:13), sometimes referred to as "the tax collector" (Matthew 10:3). After the resurrection, he is among the apostles gathered in Jerusalem (Acts 1:13).
G3156.portee: The story of Matthew shows that Jesus calls people considered undesirable or despised by religious society. As a tax collector for the Romans, Matthew was rejected by the Jews, but Jesus chose him to be an apostle. His example teaches that no one is too far away or too defiled to be transformed by the call of Jesus and become an instrument of His work. It also demonstrates the sovereign grace of God that gives unexpected gifts to those He chooses.

sens: man in the genealogy of Jesus, ancestor of Joseph
G3157.detail: Matthan is an ancestor of Jesus mentioned in the genealogy that Matthew reports at the beginning of his Gospel. He is the father of Jacob, who is the father of Joseph, the husband of Mary (Matthew 1:15).
G3157.origine: The name Matthan comes from the Hebrew מַתָּן (Mattan), which literally means "gift." It is a name that expresses the idea of what is offered or given. It is found in the Old Testament with other characters bearing the same name or variations, reflecting a naming tradition among Jewish families.
G3157.emploi: Matthan appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 1:15, in the genealogy of Jesus according to Matthew. This genealogy, which traces back from Jesus to Abraham, lists the legal ancestors of Jesus through Joseph's line. Matthan represents a link in this genealogical chain that shows how Jesus, although the Son of God, is part of the history of the people of Israel and fulfills the promises made to the ancestors.

sens: ancestor of Jesus in the genealogy of Luke
G3158G.detail: Matthat is a man mentioned in the genealogical tree of Jesus according to the Gospel of Luke. He appears as the son of Levi and the father of Melchi, listed in the long chain of ancestors that traces back from Jesus to Adam (Luke 3:24). This Hebrew name is among the generations that precede the birth of Christ, reminding us that Jesus is part of the history of the people of Israel.
G3158G.origine: The name comes from the Hebrew מַתָּת (mattath), which means "gift" or "present." It is a name rich in meaning within the biblical tradition, celebrating divine generosity. The genealogical context of Luke presents him as a link in the chain that connects Jesus to his ancestors.
G3158G.emploi: Matthat appears only once in the New Testament, in the genealogy of Jesus in Luke 3:24. Luke provides a complete genealogy of Jesus tracing back to Adam, which differs from Matthew's genealogy that goes back to Abraham. Matthat is presented as the son of Levi and the father of Melchi, placing Jesus in the history of the people of Israel and showing that He truly belongs to the human and Israelite lineage.

sens: ancestor of Jesus in the genealogy of Luke
G3158H.detail: Matthat is a character from the Old Testament whose name appears in the genealogy of Jesus reported by Luke. He is a link in the chain of Jesus' ancestors, situated several generations before His birth. In Luke 3:29, he is mentioned as the great-great-grandfather of Jesus: Jesus was the son of Joseph, the son of Heli, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, and so on back to Adam.
G3158H.origine: The Hebrew name מַתָּת (Matthat) literally means "gift" or "present" — a name that evokes a gift, which is fitting for the genealogy of one who is presented as the supreme gift of God to humanity. This name belongs to the Jewish tradition and appears in the genealogical records of Israel.
G3158H.emploi: Matthat appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:29, in the complete genealogy of Jesus that Luke traces from Joseph back to Adam. This genealogical list shows that Jesus is part of the history of Israel and that He descends from the lineage of Levi, through this family branch. Matthat is one of the many ancestors listed to establish that Jesus did not appear by chance, but that His coming is rooted in the history of God's people.

sens: Disciple of Jesus chosen to replace Judas among the twelve apostles
G3159.detail: Matthias is one of the disciples of Jesus chosen to complete the apostolic college after the betrayal and death of Judas Iscariot. After the resurrection and ascension of Jesus, the apostles gathered in Jerusalem to elect someone to take Judas' place. Two candidates were presented: Joseph called Barsabbas, also known as Justus, and Matthias (Acts 1:23). The apostles prayed, then cast lots, and the lot fell on Matthias, who then became one of the twelve apostles (Acts 1:26).
G3159.origine: The name Matthias is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Mattay or Matthaï, which means "gift of God" (from mattân, "gift"). It is a name also borne by Matthew, one of the twelve apostles, who is also called Levi. The choice of a new member for the group of apostles shows the importance that the early community placed on this fundamental role.
G3159.emploi: Matthias appears only twice in the New Testament, exclusively in chapter 1 of Acts. He is presented there as a disciple who accompanied Jesus throughout His earthly ministry, which qualified him to replace Judas. Unlike the other apostles, no specific account of his mission or later fate is reported in the Scriptures. For this reason, he is primarily known as the one who was elected the twelfth apostle by casting lots.
G3159.portee: The choice of Matthias illustrates how the early Church viewed the college of twelve as essential, as it sought to complete it from the very beginning. It also shows that the role of apostle was tied to direct knowledge of the risen Christ and a special calling, not merely to human election: it was through prayer and casting lots that the apostles entrusted this crucial decision to God.

sens: Character in the lineage of David mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus
G3160.detail: Mattatha is an ancestor of Jesus according to the lineage traced by Luke. He appears in the genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:31) as the son of Melea and the father of Menna, both descendants of David. This character lived several generations before the incarnation of Christ and is part of the genealogical chain that establishes that Jesus comes from the royal house of David.
G3160.origine: The name Mattatha is of Hebrew origin (מַתַּתָּה). It literally means "gift of the Lord" or "gift of God" (composed of "matath" = gift and the divine name). This name evokes God's grace and kindness towards this lineage.
G3160.emploi: Mattatha appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:31. Luke mentions him in the detailed genealogy of Jesus, also known as the "genealogy of Joseph." This genealogy traces from Jesus back to Adam, passing through David and Nathan (son of David). Mattatha occupies a specific place in this succession of generations that highlights the historical continuity of God's plan.

sens: Man in the genealogy of Jesus mentioned in the Gospel of Luke
G3161G.detail: Mattathias is an ancestor of Jesus according to the genealogy reported by Luke in chapter 3 of his Gospel. He appears in this long list of names that traces from Jesus back to Adam, thus placing Jesus in the continuity of the entire history of God's people. His name means "gift of Yahweh" in Hebrew.
G3161G.origine: The name Mattathias comes from the Hebrew Mattithyahu, formed from "mat" (gift) and "Yahu" (Yahweh). It is a name bearing a divine promise: the one who bears it is a gift from God. This same root is found in other biblical names like Matthew, which also means "gift of Yahweh." The name appears in the genealogies of the Old Testament in similar forms.
G3161G.emploi: Mattathias appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:25, in the genealogy of Jesus according to Luke. He is presented as the father of Amos and the son of Nahum. This genealogical list is unique to Luke among the Gospels; it is more developed than that of Matthew and traces back to Adam to emphasize the universality of the salvation brought by Jesus. Mattathias himself is not a character named in the biblical narratives; he represents a link in the genealogical chain.

sens: Ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy
G3161H.detail: Mattathias is a name borne by an ancestor of Jesus according to the genealogy reported by Luke in chapter 3. He appears as the father of Maath in this long list of the Lord's ancestors (Luke 3:26). He is a link in the genealogical chain that connects Jesus to Adam, showing how the Son of God fits into the history of God's people.
G3161H.origine: The name Mattathias comes from Hebrew and means "gift of Yahweh" (from Mattath, "gift," and Yah, the name of God). It is a name that expresses trust in divine generosity, borne by several important figures in Israel's history, including the founder of the Maccabean revolt in the 2nd century BC.
G3161H.emploi: Mattathias appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:26, in the genealogy of Jesus. Luke traces the generations from Jesus back to Adam, thus placing Christ in the complete history of God's people. This name appears among the more distant ancestors, distinct from the royal line of David, and testifies to how the two genealogies (that of Luke and that of Matthew) differently trace the descent of Jesus.

sens: Large knife or blade for sacrifice
Short sword or dagger, combat weapon
Warrior's weapon, power to kill
Killing edge, deadly blow
Figuratively: word of God that judges
Instrument of division or conflict
G3162.detail:
1. In the Old Testament and early biblical narratives, the machaira primarily refers to a large knife used for sacrifices: Abraham carries one to offer his son Isaac (Genesis 22:6, 10).
2. It later becomes a combat weapon — a short sword or dagger — carried by Roman soldiers and the disciples. Peter draws one to cut off the ear of the high priest's servant when Jesus is arrested (Matthew 26:51, John 18:10).
3. The sword represents the power to wage war and kill: the horsemen of the Apocalypse carry them, and Romans 13:4 reminds that the magistrate "bears the sword" to punish evil (Romans 13:4, Acts 12:2).
4. The expression "the edge of the sword" refers to violent death in battle: thus Luke 21:24 announces that the Jews "will fall by the edge of the sword."
5. In Hebrews 4:12, the Word of God is compared to "a two-edged sword" — it penetrates to the most hidden thoughts of the heart to judge them.
6. Jesus declares: "I did not come to bring peace, but a sword" (Matthew 10:34), an image of the conflict and division that his coming provokes.
G3162.origine: The Greek word μάχαιρα comes from the ancient Greek world and translates the Hebrew חֶרֶב (herev), which also means "sword." These two words share the image of a sharp blade, and the Hebrew root evokes the idea of separation, division. In Greek, μάχαιρα is opposed to ῥομφαία (a broad sword) and ξίφος (a straight combat sword). It is a common word in ancient Greek for any portable bladed weapon.
G3162.emploi: The word machaira appears 26 times in the New Testament. It first refers to the weapon that the disciples and soldiers carry during Jesus' arrest (Matthew 26:47-55, Mark 14:43-48, Luke 22:36-52, John 18:10-11). It then describes the sword of the Roman magistrate, a symbol of his authority to punish (Romans 13:4, Acts 16:27). The biblical text also uses it for violent death in battle, particularly in prophecies of destruction (Luke 21:24, Revelation 6:4, 13:10).
